item.title: [Sportsnaut] MLB Insider Claims Phillies Will 'Kick Around Idea' of Bryce Harper Trade This Winter: 5 Potential Landing Spots, Including the NY Yankees
item.dc:creator: Jasonburgosmma; Jason Burgos

item.content:encoded:
After a disappointing end to the 2026 season, a prominent MLB insider believes the Philadelphia Phillies will consider trading long-time star Bryce Harper this winter.
The Phillies entered this year with the fourth-highest payroll in MLB and big expectations. While they didn’t win the National League East, the hope was that their talent-rich roster could still go on a deep run in the postseason. Unfortunately, despite their best efforts, Philadelphia came up short in their three-game Wild Card series against division rivals the Atlanta Braves.
Following their season-ending loss on Thursday, The Athletic’s Ken Rosenthal claimed, “The Phillies at least need to kick around the idea of trading” the All-Star first baseman. A player the MLB insider feels doesn’t have an “oppressive” contract, with five years and $118 million left on the deal.
If the team pulled the trigger on a trade for the two-time NL MVP this winter, here are five teams he could end up landing with this winter.
Chicago Cubs
The Chicago Cubs had an equally frustrating finish to their 2026 campaign this week as well. However, they didn’t even get to three games, and the team with the sixth highest payroll in baseball was soundly beaten by the San Diego Padres in just two.
Chicago could lose both of their corner outfielders this winter, so Harper could fill either of those spots. Or the nine-time All-Star could be an option at DH. Either way, Harper would be a really nice addition to the lineup. Plus, like Alex Bregman, he is a strong veteran leader and player in the postseason.
Boston Red Sox
The Boston Red Sox are another team that saw their playoff run ended in just two games. In their case, it was rivals the New York Yankees who eliminated them. Harper could certainly be an option for Boston at DH. But the thing this team lacks the most, which he would address, is a proven veteran leader on the field and in the clubhouse. If he can handle the pressure of Philadelphia, Harper would be fine in Boston.
Toronto Blue Jays
This season was a massive disappointment for the Toronto Blue Jays. After being a couple of outs away from winning the World Series last fall, the Jays finished dead last in the AL East with a 79-83 record this year. So you can bet they will look to make a big move this offseason to get back into title contention in 2027.
If the Phillies actually make Harper available in trade talks, Toronto will be fascinated by the idea of pairing him with Vladimir Guerrero Jr. next season. If Guerrero Jr. can return to the player he always has been in 2027, and Kazuma Okamoto puts up similar power numbers, adding Harper to the batting order gives Toronto a spot in the order you can’t pitch around.
New York Yankees
The Yankees are still in the race to be champions in 2026. However, if they fall short of that yearly goal, the Yanks will surely look into adding a piece or two that can get them to end their 17-year title drought.
New York would need to find a new home for Giancarlo Stanton, but with only one guaranteed season for $15 million left on his deal, it may be possible this offseason. If they can trade the injury-prone five-time All-Star, a lineup with a healthy Aaron Judge, Harper, Ben Rice, and Cody Bellinger is one of the best in baseball.
St. Louis Cardinals
While the St. Louis Cardinals finished 77-85 this season, they seemed a bit ahead of schedule in their rebuild because of the upside in young stars JJ Wetherholt and Jordan Walker. The Cards are willing to make bold moves for proven stars if they feel they can help get the team to the next level or change the culture for the better. Harper could do both.
With St. Louis having a top-five farm system in MLB, they would certainly have the prospect assets to easily get a deal done.

item.title: [PhillyVoice] This era of the Phillies feels like it's over

item.content:encoded:
October 02, 2026
Ryan Howard twisted uncomfortably out of the batter's box, then crumpled just a few steps down the first-base line as the St. Louis Cardinals rushed toward the mound to celebrate.
An October-fueled Citizens Bank Park fell silent.
The Phillies had lost Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS, and suddenly, shockingly, their all-in chase after another World Series title was over.
Roy Halladay, with his last bit of true greatness, tossed a one-run gem that should've been enough of a chance, and yet was nullified by an even more brilliant complete game from Chris Carpenter, who made a Philadelphia lineup flush with high-profile bats look entirely pedestrian.
And then there was Howard at the end, the star slugger who was left lying there in the grass as the Phillies' grand ambitions all came crashing down.
No one wanted to say it out loud at the time. Maybe they just couldn't bring themselves to fully accept it just yet. But that image has since been permanently etched into the minds of every Phillies fan who witnessed it, because deep down, everyone knew right then and there: A golden era of Phillies baseball was over.
One by one, the generation defined by Howard, Jimmy Rollins, Chase Utley, Cole Hamels, that second-ever World Championship in 2008, and then Halladay, Cliff Lee, and any other big name that the organization could get its hands on in the pursuit of one more, faded.
Those Phillies were never competitive again.
Bryce Harper whiffed on a low and way, way away slider from Chris Sale that he never had a prayer of hitting, and that Drake Baldwin, behind the plate, never had a prayer of catching.
Harper, slowly and totally unaware, bent down to take his shin guard off, thinking it was strike three and that the inning was over. He never saw the ball spike past Baldwin in the dirt, and go rolling to the backstop. By the time he realized, all he gave was a disinterested jog up the first base line, which did finally end the eighth inning from Baldwin having the time to recover for the throw up to the base.
John Kruk: "RUN!"
Bryce Harper was slow to get out of the box, not realizing strike three had gotten away.
(Via: @MLB) pic.twitter.com/GRcx3VGWtQ
— Foul Territory (@FoulTerritoryTV) October 2, 2026
The Phillies were down, 6-2, in the deciding Game 3 of the 2026 NL Wild Card series, on the road against the rival Atlanta Braves.
They still had three outs of life left, but everyone watching knew full well – and probably had no hesitation admitting this time, just shy of 15 years later – that another playoff era of Phillies baseball was over.
And once this club does get back to South Philadelphia, there will be no World Series pennant to look up at in center field and over Ashburn Alley.
The closest this generation ever got was that first breakout run that burnt out against the Astros in 2022.
They only ever got further away from it from there, and now might be all out of chances.
The Phillies stood in the visiting clubhouse, and interim manager Don Mattingly sat at the press conference dais.
No one spoke with any certainties.
Mattingly, who took over midseason for Rob Thomson, talked around whether he wanted to come back and how he felt about the decision the Phillies will have to make this winter for whoever their next full-time manager is going to be.
"It's not the time to talk about anything like that," Mattingly said. "...I want the Phillies to do what they need to do."
Granted, anything shy of a World Series always seemed to point toward him not staying.
Alec Bohm, the first-round and homegrown infielder who was good but always had better expected of him, is now headed for free agency and didn't want to talk about what his future held either.
Trea Turner, who certainly will be back just by the nature of his enormous 11-year, $300 million contract, knows he can't with another season like this one, where his numbers at the plate are low and where you can never be fully confident that he'll properly field the baseball. That can't cut it.
"[I] got a lot of work to do," Turner said.
And then there was Harper, who didn't have much to offer either, save for one definitive statement.
"I'd imagine this team's gonna look a lot different next year," said Harper, "with the guys that are kind of leaving this clubhouse. We'll see."
If there even is a next year for baseball.
Either way, it does feel like this team has to be.
The next few weeks are undoubtedly going to put the Phillies and everyone responsible for their current construction up to harsh scrutiny, amid a fan base that, really, got tired of them two postseason failures ago.
Dave Dombrowski, the Phillies' president of baseball operations, will have the most to answer for, after he repeatedly ran it back with an aging core, failed once again to put together a competent bullpen, and ended this season with none of his trade deadline acquisitions on the postseason roster, all while presiding over a barren-looking farm system.
Hitting coach Kevin Long, who has long been immune from any other shifts in the dugout staff around him, has to face the music here, too, after the Phillies continued to have a collectively abysmal approach at the plate – outside of a month – and after seeing nearly all of the Phils' batters either plateau, regress, or in the case of Luis Arráez, to see a perennial .300-plus hitter suddenly drop well below that line the second he put on a red-pinstriped uniform.
And then there's Harper, the big face of an era that kept falling short and now might not even be good enough to get there to begin with anymore.
All offseason and into spring training, it was clear he was miffed by Dombrowski openly questioning to the press last fall whether he could be "elite" anymore.
Harper said back in February that it wasn't something to motivate him, but he made it obvious, too, that those remarks stuck in his craw.
And he would go on to put up solid numbers, and yeah, he even had his heroics in a Game 2 that kept the Phillies alive for another day.
But now they're done. This era might be done, and with its end forever tied to that moment of Harper leisurely taking his shin guard off at the plate, not knowing the ball went rolling, and by the time he did, not having enough care to even try to fully run it out.
It felt a lot like Ryan Howard 15 years ago. It felt like an era was over.
This one, though, might be a bit more bitter.
*QUOTES SOURCE: NBC Sports Philadelphia on YouTube

item.content:encoded:
Phillies get ridiculous Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber trade suggestion from MLB insider originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
Philadelphia Phillies fans were, once again, let down by the team in 2026. They lost Game 3 of the NL Wild Card to the Atlanta Braves, getting eliminated in the first round of the postseason for the third straight season.
So much went wrong this season, and the writing was on the wall with this team. But that doesn't change how tough it was to see this Phillies team lose another series, this time to the division rival Braves.
A lot of changes need to be made to this organization if they want to contend. Some of those changes might be unpopular. But the suggestion from Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic to try and trade either Bryce Harper or Kyle Schwarber is completely ridiculous.
Phillies get ridiculous Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber trade suggestion from MLB insider
"Trading Bryce Harper or Kyle Schwarber? Don't love the idea, but everything needs to be under consideration. Everything," Rosenthal writes. "... The Phillies at least need to kick around the idea of trading one of them."
Rosenthal believes that the Phillies need to make some major changes this offseason, which is a sentiment likely many Phillies fans share.
But trading Schwarber or Harper would be a step too far. There are some bold moves that would actually make sense for this team, like trading Brandon Marsh. A trade involving Harper or Schwarber would not make any sense.
Sure, the Phillies would likely get a haul for either slugger, free up a lot of money in the process, and hope for a culture-resetting move.
Maybe this idea works on paper. In practice, trading Harper or Schwarber would be a horrendous idea. They are easily the best hitters on this Phillies team, and both are signed for at least the next four years with full no-trade clauses.
There is no scenario in which trading Harper or Schwarber would make sense for this Phillies team if they have any intention of competing next year.
Unless the Phillies decide to completely blow the team up and enter a full-scale rebuild, a trade of either beloved superstar would be a misguided effort from the Phillies.
While changes have to be made for this franchise to get back to being a serious postseason threat, there is no scenario in which Schwarber or Harper should be traded.
This suggestion from Rosenthal is a horrible one, and there's zero reason Dave Dombrowski or Jon Middleton should ever sign off on a trade of either player. If either is dealt, they might as well tear this team apart for prospects and stop trying to contend.

item.title: [CBS Sports] Should the Phillies trade Bryce Harper or Kyle Schwarber? Why blockbuster deal doesn't make sense

item.content:encoded:
The Phillies were bounced from the playoffs with a Game 3 Wild Card Series loss to the Braves on Thursday night. Given that the Phillies made the World Series in 2022 and have regressed in playoff performance since (NLCS in 2023, NLDS in 2024, NLDS in 2025 and WCS in 2026) along with a relatively old roster, there has been a stream of "end of an era" discussion on Friday.
It's not unreasonable. There are certainly . There are bound to be overreactions. I overreact a decent amount of the time, so I get it. It happens. We're often prisoners of the moment and emotion is a real thing.
I do want to push back on a specific idea, though, as floated by Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic:
Trading Bryce Harper or Kyle Schwarber? Don't love the idea, but everything needs to be under consideration. Everything.
Now, be sure that this isn't to attack the writer there, as I have the utmost respect for him and he even said he doesn't love the idea. I can see a lot of people running with this, though, and I'll offer up my opinion that this just isn't a feasible idea for the Phillies.
First off, Harper has a no-trade clause and it's been pretty clear over the last several years that he's now Philly through-and-through and doesn't want to go anywhere. Schwarber also has a no-trade clause with his 10-and-5 rights and now has a family with two young children.
Let's say either or both would accept a trade. Would it help the Phillies other than salary relief?
Schwarber is a 34-year-old designated hitter heading into 2027 with four years and $132 million left on his deal. How many teams would give the Phillies anything of value while also taking on a large portion of the salary? The answer is not that many and it might be zero.
Harper needs to permanently go back to first base and he'll also be 34 years old next season. He has five years and roughly $125 million left on his deal. Again, how many teams would give good value back to the Phillies and salary relief? The number is higher than with Schwarber, but not by much.
This isn't to say neither player is good. Both are very productive offensively. In fact, they were the Phillies' only two good hitters this season. Harper had a 131 OPS+ and Schwarber was at 128 with 100 being the average player at getting on base and hitting for power. No other qualified players on the Phillies were in the vicinity of Harper or Schwarber. Only Bryson Stott at 98 even approached league average. Brandon Marsh finished at 90, Alec Bohm 87 and Trea Turner 81. Yuck.
Schwarber and Harper are much more valuable to the Phillies than they would be to any other team, given the circumstances. And, unless the Phillies are going full-on rebuild, they might as well play out the contracts and try to win with them.
If you look at how things are set up for next season with the pitching staff, a rebuild doesn't make sense.
- Jesús Luzardo made a turn toward ace this season. He's under team control through at least 2031.
- Cristopher Sánchez will likely finish in the top three of Cy Young voting. He's under team control through at least 2032.
- Zack Wheeler showed flashes of being really good while returning from an incredibly tough surgical procedure. He's signed for one more season. He could well return to ace form.
- Aaron Nola doesn't have a tradeable deal, but hey, he had a 10-start stretch with a 2.10 ERA late in the season.
- There were still inconsistencies, but Andrew Painter, at age 23, made big strides during the season and perhaps turned a corner with in Game 2 vs. the Braves. Next year could well be a breakout.
That's a five-man rotation and maybe one of the very best in the majors.
Jhoan Duran is a top-three closer, too.
The starting point here is a great rotation and closer combination, along with Harper and Schwarber being excellent hitters. That's a better nucleus than most teams have. Ownership is committed to doing what it takes to land a winner for the city of Philadelphia and Dave Dombrowski is a front office executive who has proven he's good at making good teams into champions.
Keep taking as many shots at the postseason as possible in hopes that one of these years, the hot streak lines up properly for a championship. We've seen a well-timed hot streak pay off in recent years for teams like the Nationals, Braves and Rangers -- and maybe it'll be the Padres this year? -- so we know it can happen. Hell, the 2022 Phillies were right there.
The team defense needs to improve and there should be some tinkering with the position players, but the foundation here is far too strong to bail on Schwarber and/or Harper, especially when it wouldn't improve the big-league roster in the near-term.

item.content:encoded:
Ranking Phillies 2B Luis Arraez's Top 5 Landing Spots Ahead of MLB Free Agency
Any club pursuing three-time batting champion Luis Arraez will likely need a plan to play him regularly at second base.
In a 2026 season split between the San Francisco Giants and Philadelphia Phillies, Arraez returned to his natural position of second base. In terms of outs above average, he had the best season of his career, with San Francisco infield coach Ron Washington credited with helping his defensive growth.
Arraez should do better this offseason than the one-year, $12 million deal he settled for last offseason. He was unavailable for the Phillies' Wild Card Series loss to Atlanta because of a sprained left ankle, though the injury is not expected to affect his availability for 2027.
Let's take a look at the best potential landing spots for the four-time All-Star.
5. Texas Rangers
1 of 5
Whether the Rangers are in on Arraez will depend on whether managing partner Ray Davis authorizes president of baseball operations Chris Young to add payroll in the offseason.
From a baseball perspective, the Rangers' second basemen posted an OPS south of .700 this season. Clearly, Arraez would give them more offensively than they got in 2026.
Top prospect Sebastian Walcott is a shortstop/third baseman who is expected to play a role for the team in 2027. But even with Corey Seager at shortstop and Josh Jung at third base, Walcott seems more likely to play outfield than second base. There aren't many 6'4" second basemen.
4. Philadelphia Phillies
2 of 5
Arraez didn't perform as well with the Phillies as he did with the Giants, but his track record suggests that over a larger sample size, he will hit for a higher average.
The Phillies dealt pitching prospects Ramon Marquez and Marty Gair to acquire Arraez and reliever Caleb Kilian, so they should at least consider a reunion in free agency.
That said, some of this will come down to how the Phillies want to set up their infield in 2027. Alec Bohm will likely depart in free agency, while Bryce Harper is expected to return to first base.
Will the Phillies move Trea Turner off of shortstop, and if so will that be to second base or left field? What about Bryson Stott, whom the team likes at second base but moved to third to accommodate Arraez? Also looming is top prospect Aidan Miller, who missed most of 2026 but is an exciting bat who can play shortstop or third base.
Many moving parts make it unclear whether the Phillies will commit to multiple seasons of Arraez at second base. Still, his presence behind Bryce Harper gave Philadelphia a contact-oriented option in the heart of its lineup and may have made it easier for Harper to remain selective at the plate.
3. Pittsburgh Pirates
3 of 5
Will the Pirates extend the qualifying offer to Brandon Lowe? It's always difficult to know how owner Bob Nutting will operate. Even if the QO goes to Lowe, one would think he'd decline it in search of a multi-year commitment.
If Lowe ends up not returning to Pittsburgh, the Buccos will have a hole at second base. One way to soften the negative reaction to not bringing Lowe back after an excellent contract year is to sign a replacement as accomplished as Arraez.
You could do worse than a middle-infield pairing of Arraez and Konnor Griffin, especially in terms of offensive production.
2. San Francisco Giants
4 of 5
It's rare but not unheard of for a player to get traded midseason and then return to the club that traded him in the offseason as a free agent. This might be one of the instances where it makes sense, though.
Arraez not only built a great relationship with the aforementioned Washington, but he also hit .324 in 105 games with the Giants. While home run hitters other than Barry Bonds don't love Oracle Park, Arraez's offensive profile fit the park well. In 49 games at Oracle Park in 2026, Arraez hit .361.
This may come down to whether the Giants are comfortable with Casey Schmitt playing elsewhere on the diamond so Arraez can resume as the team's second baseman. Offensively, Arraez remains a great fit for the Giants.
1. Detroit Tigers
5 of 5
The Tigers will have quite a bit of money coming off the books this offseason, including the $22.025 million that Gleyber Torres made after accepting the qualifying offer last winter.
Arraez spent the first four seasons of his career with the Minnesota Twins, so a return to the AL Central could make sense. It's a bit surprising that Arraez has hit only .265 in 88 career plate appearances at Comerica Park, but the spacious outfield suits a contact hitter.
Additionally, with Torres coming off the books, the Tigers will have an opening at second base. Adding Arraez's bat-to-ball skills could help Detroit rebound from a disappointing 2026.

item.title: [si.com] Unlikely Hero Ray Kerr Silences Phillies As Braves Advance to NLDS

item.content:encoded:
The Braves powered their way to an NLDS berth after taking out their division rivals.
On Thursday night, Atlanta won a winner-take-all Game 3 against the Phillies, 6–2, in front of a loud Truist Park crowd. The Braves tagged Philadelphia starter Aaron Nola for three runs in the bottom of the first inning and never looked back, leading wire-to-wire to eliminate their NL East peers.
Surprise starter Ray Kerr, a 32-year-old with 72 2/3 career MLB innings, pitched into the fourth inning unscathed to keep the Phillies at arm’s length. The Phillies never found much offense beyond contributions from stars Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber, as the supporting cast beyond Alec Bohm failed to step up.
The victory sends Atlanta to Los Angeles for an NLDS matchup with the Dodgers starting on Saturday. For Philadelphia, a season that began with World Series ambitions was cut short in the wild-card round.
Here are our three takeaways from Game 3.
Braves Slug Their Way to NLDS
Atlanta relied heavily on the long ball in 2026, and with its season on the line that’s what it used to punch a ticket to the NLDS.
The Braves’ 204 regular season home runs ranked seventh in baseball, while their collective .409 slugging percentage was sixth. In Game 3, they flexed those muscles, blasting three home runs that accounted for each of their six runs.
Michael Harris II got things started in the bottom of the first, when he stepped to the plate with one out after back-to-back walks to Ronald Acuña Jr. and Matt Olson. He hammered a 2–0 sinker from Aaron Nola just over the right field wall to give Atlanta a 3–0 lead it wouldn’t relinquish.
Ozzie Albies got into the act three innings later when he launched a 96 mph four-seamer from Zack Wheeler 419 feet into the stands in right-center to increase the lead to 5–0.
Matt Olson added another in the seventh inning when he crushed a Jonathan Bowlan changeup to center to give Atlanta a 6–1 margin.
If the Braves are going to make a deep run in the playoffs, they’ll need to keep thumping baseballs out of the park. It’s the way they have played all year and it's how they were able to close out the Phillies.
The Ray Kerr Game
When the Braves announced their Game 3 starter, the collective response from the baseball world was: “Who?” We all know his name now.
Kerr had a remarkable path to signing with the Mariners as an undrafted free agent in 2017, at different points working at a movie theater and a 7-Eleven after dropping out of junior college. He bounced around the minors for several years and finally made his big league debut for the Padres at 27 years old in ’22, then recorded a 5.06 ERA in 29 games (32 innings) out of the bullpen over two seasons. He was then traded to Atlanta and recorded a 5.64 ERA in 10 games for Atlanta in 2024, but didn’t get back to the majors until Aug. 17 of this year. Once he did, he shined.
In nine appearances, he was 1–0 with a 1.47 ERA and a 0.60 WHIP. Still, he had three career starts entering Thursday night, and his team had never won any of them. The 32-year-old lefty made Atlanta manager Walt Weiss look like a genius Thursday night.
In his postseason debut, Kerr was locked in on the mound as he carved through a Phillies lineup loaded with All-Stars. He pitched 3 ⅓ shutout innings, allowing one hit, one walk and striking out two. Kerr left the game with a 3–0 lead. Atlanta’s rotation is banged up right now and they needed a big performance from whoever started Game 3. They got it from the last guy anyone expected.
Schwarber, Harper Get No Help
Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper brought the Phillies back from the dead in Game 2, hammering back-to-back home runs in the eighth inning to tie a game Philadelphia ultimately won in 10 innings. On Thursday night in Game 3, the duo combined to go 3-for-7 with a walk and a run scored. The rest of the lineup went 3-for-24 with two walks and a run. That wasn’t going to get it done.
As a team, the Phillies slashed .231/.270/.394 with 23 strikeouts over the three games, while Trea Turner went 1-for-11, Bryson Stott was 2-for-13 and J.T. Realmuto was 2-for-10. Alec Bohm was the only other hitter who showed up, going 4-for-12 with a home run. The offense that ranked 28th in wRC+ (92) during the regular season didn’t give enough support to its two main contributors, as the flaws that dogged the Phillies all year were predictably their undoing as they exited the postseason with a whimper.
If Philadelphia is going to keep its title window open, Schwarber and Harper need some help.
Ryan Phillips is a senior writer on the Breaking and Trending News team at Sports Illustrated. He has worked in digital media since 2009, spending eight years at The Big Lead before joining SI in 2024. Phillips also co-hosts The Assembly Call Podcast about Indiana Hoosiers basketball and previously worked at Bleacher Report. He is a proud San Diego native and a graduate of Indiana University’s journalism program.

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA (AP) — Bryce Harper no quiere pronunciar frases que comiencen con “si hubiera", “si pudiera” o ”debí haber".
La conclusión para los Filis de Filadelfia es que volvieron a quedarse cortos en la postemporada.
“Estamos aquí para hacer el trabajo. Estamos aquí para ganar juegos y no lo hicimos”, comentó Harper en un apagado clubhouse de los Filis la noche del jueves, tras su derrota por 6-2 ante los Bravos de Atlanta en el tercer y decisivo encuentro de su serie de comodines de la Liga Nacional:
El toletero estelar no puso excusas por el bajón de septiembre que impidió a los Filis alinear su pitcheo contra Atlanta, porque necesitaron hasta el juego número 162 para asegurar un puesto en los playoffs.
Filadelfia forzó el tercer juego ante los Bravo con tres dramáticos jonrones solitarios en la recta final del segundo encuentro. Pero al final, los Filis cayeron en un hoyo temprano en el partido del jueves y quedaron eliminados de la postemporada por quinto año consecutivo, mientras persiguen su primer título de la Serie Mundial desde 2008.
Al mánager interino Don Mattingly le habría encantado poder organizar el pitcheo y que estuviera descansado y todo eso.
“Pero no fue así. Tuvimos que pelear para meternos, y para hacer lo que teníamos que hacer para entrar, tuvimos que hacerlo básicamente en cada juego de la serie”, señaló.
El núcleo de los Filis —Harper, Kyle Schwarber, J.T. Realmuto, Zack Wheeler y Aaron Nola— ha llegado a los playoffs cinco años seguidos y promedió 91 victorias por temporada en ese tramo. Aún no han ganado un campeonato y cada año Filadelfia se ha quedado más lejos de ese objetivo desde que alcanzó la Serie Mundial de 2022.
La temporada siguiente, se despidió en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional, y los dos años posteriores terminaron con derrotas en la serie divisional. Una eliminación en comodines esta temporada representa otro paso en la dirección equivocada.
“Obviamente, nos encantaría ganar una Serie Mundial con estos muchachos. Hemos estado juntos bastante tiempo, tenemos un buen clubhouse y, ya sabes, buenos tipos en este equipo", manifestó Nola. "Sabemos qué clase de personas hay aquí. Sabemos qué clase de peloteros tenemos y de lo que somos capaces. Necesitamos jugar bien en el momento adecuado”.
La racha de cinco años incluyó dos triunfos de serie de playoffs sobre los Bravos. Filadelfia eliminó a Atlanta en 2022 y 2023 pese a que los Bravos ganaron el Este de la Liga Nacional en ambas temporadas. Ese escenario se repitió este año: los Bravos obtuvieron la ventaja de local en esta serie gracias a otro título del Este de la Liga Nacional.
Esta vez, sin embargo, Atlanta consiguió los batazos grandes y el pitcheo oportuno. Ray Kerr, en apenas su décima aparición del año y su primera de postemporada, cumplió a la perfección el papel de abridor. Lanzó 3 1/3 entradas, sin permitir carreras, con una base por bolas y un hit, para preparar el relevo largo de Grant Holmes.
Michael Harris II conectó un jonrón de tres carreras ante Nola en la primera entrada, y los Filis estuvieron a la zaga el resto de la noche.
Estuvieron abajo en su división en abril, pero con el tiempo enderezaron el rumbo. Mattingly asumió el mando cuando Rob Thomson fue despedido el 28 de abril tras un inicio de 9-18.
Los Filis ganaron ocho de sus siguientes nueve juegos y llegaron a .500 el 16 de mayo. Un agosto al rojo vivo los puso en posición de playoffs, pero el boleto de postemporada no se aseguró sino hasta el último juego de la temporada regular.
Mattingly esquivó las preguntas sobre su futuro después del partido.
“No es el momento de hablar de eso. Me siento cómodo con lo que quieran hacer. De nuevo, quiero lo mejor para los Filis. Me encantó estar en Filadelfia este año", indicó. "De hecho, me gusta jugar en ese ambiente. Me gusta el ambiente. Es un ambiente duro, pero es bueno. Otra vez, creo que dejas que la organización evalúe, hable sobre lo que piensa de cara al futuro, lo que debería hacer, y eso determina muchas cosas diferentes”.

item.title: [Bleacher Report] Bryce Harper Talks Future After Playoff Elimination, Phillies 'Will Look a Lot Different' in 2027
item.dc:creator: Andrew Peters
item.description: Bryce Harper Talks Future After Playoff Elimination, Phillies 'Will Look a Lot Different' in 2027 The Philadelphia Phillies' season ended in the American League Wild Card round on Thursday after a 6-2 loss to the Atlanta Braves. item.content:encoded:
Bryce Harper Talks Future After Playoff Elimination, Phillies 'Will Look a Lot Different' in 2027
The Philadelphia Phillies' season ended in the American League Wild Card round on Thursday after a 6-2 loss to the Atlanta Braves.
The Phillies have plenty of questions heading into the offseason, and Bryce Harper expects the team to "look a lot different" in 2027.
"Each year's so different than the year before. I don't really put stock into years before or what happened or anything else," Harper said. "This was a brand new team. Obviously, we had the guys that are part of that core group that we are. I'd imagine this team is going to look a lot different next year with the guys that are leaving this clubhouse. So, we'll see."
Harper is tied to the Phillies through the 2031 season, so he'll remain in Philadelphia for years to come, barring a trade. Stars like Zack Wheeler, Kyle Schwarber, Trea Turner and Aaron Nola are also set to return.
But the Phillies have a handful of notable free agents, such as Alec Bohm, Jose Alvarado, Luis Arreaz, Emundo Sosa and more.
Perhaps the biggest question mark is who will be the Phillies' skipper in 2027.
Philadelphia fired manager Rob Thomson in April after a rough start to the season, and interim manager Don Mattingly helped the Phillies get back on track to reach the postseason, but he has yet to shed the interim tag.
Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic reported this week that Mattingly was "likely to be replaced" if the Phillies didn't make a deep run in the postseason, so it seems Philadelphia will be on the hunt for a new manager.
Schwarber spoke highly of Mattingly after the season ended on Thursday.
"Even when things got hard, the way that he was able to keep things at even-keel pace for us. I think that was huge," Schwarber said.
The Phillies were interested in Alex Cora after he was fired by the Boston Red Sox, but he turned the offer down. Cora said in April that he's interested in getting back into baseball at some point, but didn't clarify how soon that would be.
Even with an offseason full of changes coming, the Phillies will retain most of their core as they try to get back to the World Series. How different the team will look in the spring remains to be seen.

item.title: [MLB.com] Sale's pitch to Weiss pays off: Lefty bookends Braves' Wild Card Series win
item.dc:creator: Paul Casella
item.description: The Braves' ace had an important matter to address before Game 3 of the National League Wild Card Series on Thursday night at Truist Park. "First of all, I was not going to go to Chris Sale and ask him if he could pitch tonight," Weiss said after the Braves’ series-clinching 6-2 win. "I didn't want to put him in that position, because I knew that, even if he was hanging, he would tell me yes. So I was not going to bring it up." Turns out, Weiss didn't need to. "Literally as soon as I stepped in
item.content:encoded:
The Braves' ace had an important matter to address before Game 3 of the National League Wild Card Series on Thursday night at Truist Park.
"First of all, I was not going to go to Chris Sale and ask him if he could pitch tonight," Weiss said after the Braves’ series-clinching 6-2 win. "I didn't want to put him in that position, because I knew that, even if he was hanging, he would tell me yes. So I was not going to bring it up."
Turns out, Weiss didn't need to.
"Literally as soon as I stepped in my office this afternoon, he was sitting in the chair across from my desk," Weiss said. "And he looked at me and he said, 'I feel amazing.'”
Weiss’ response?
“Well, let's talk."
From there, the two laid out a plan that ultimately saw Sale take down the final four outs of the Braves' first postseason series win since the 2021 World Series. Keep in mind, Sale also recorded the club's first 19 outs of this Wild Card Series as the Game 1 starter in Atlanta's 5-3 victory two days earlier.
In doing so, Sale became the first pitcher to start Game 1 of a postseason series and finish off that same series since ... Chris Sale. He previously did the same thing for the Red Sox in the 2018 World Series against the Dodgers.
Sale joined Clayton Kershaw as the only pitchers to accomplish the feat multiple times in postseason history.
"What a warrior, man," Weiss said. "This guy -- I've run out of superlatives for Chris Sale. Been talking about him all year. He's one of the best I've ever been around."
Even with Sale’s mid-afternoon ambush opening up some options for Weiss, their meticulously crafted plan only worked if all of the pieces fell into place.
Ray Kerr had to go out and do his job as the opener. Grant Holmes had to take it from there and relay the torch to a trio of relievers -- Robert Suarez, Didier Fuentes and Dylan Dodd -- who each had to take care of business.
And even then, the offense also needed to do its part. Michael Harris II checked that box early with a three-run homer in the first inning, then Ozzie Albies (a two-run shot in the fourth) and Matt Olson (a solo blast in the seventh) tacked on.
"Unbelievable. I'm just thankful for the opportunity, honestly," Sale said. "This could not be more of a group effort. This was basically a culmination of our entire year. All hands on deck. Everyone is doing everything they can to just get a win for this team."
Safe to say everything went to plan?
Well, sort of.
Knowing the plan was to pitch against the top of the Phillies' order in either the eighth or the ninth inning, Sale started to throw in the bullpen in the top of the seventh. But when Olson's homer extended the Braves' lead to 6-1 in the bottom of the seventh, it altered the strategy.
Even with Philadelphia's 9-1-2 hitters due up, Weiss instead went with the left-handed Dodd to start the eighth. He gave up a leadoff triple to pinch-hitter Derek Hill, who then scored on Trea Turner's sacrifice fly to cut the lead to four.
Needing to face at least three batters, Dodd had to stay in to face Kyle Schwarber -- the same guy who homered in the eighth inning off Dylan Lee one day earlier to trigger the Phillies' Game 2 comeback. Dodd was up to the task, though, getting MLB's regular-season home run leader to fly out for the second out.
Then, it was showtime: Sale vs. Bryce Harper.
"Electric," Harris said of the moment Sale emerged from the bullpen.
"The best," Albies said. "The minute I saw him getting warmed up, I said, 'He's definitely coming in. I love this.' The energy, the excitement there -- everybody was pumped that he came in the game."
Well, everyone except the Phillies.
Sale struck out Harper on four pitches, getting him to chase three sliders well out of the zone. The last one missed badly enough to go to the backstop, but catcher Drake Baldwin tracked it down to throw out Harper.
Now came another decision for Weiss: Let Sale go back out for the ninth or turn it over to closer Raisel Iglesias with a four-run lead?
With Iglesias warming just in case, the home crowd roared as Sale emerged from the dugout to trot back out for the ninth. Four batters later, the Braves had punched their ticket for an NLDS showdown with the Dodgers.
"Was hoping he only had to go one," Weiss said, "but he had to get to four outs."
All told, Sale -- the Braves' presumed starter for Sunday's Game 2 -- threw 21 pitches over 1 1/3 innings.
Is he still good to go for Sunday?
"I don't know. I have no idea," Weiss said. "We weren't even worried about that. It was just, 'Put this thing down and then we'll have those conversations later.' But yeah, we haven't even talked about that. It was all about tonight."
If Weiss has any doubts, he’ll certainly be getting another visit this weekend at Dodger Stadium.
"If I had to pitch tomorrow," Sale said, "I'd pitch tomorrow."

item.title: [Bozeman Daily Chronicle] Bryce Harper after Phillies' early playoff exit: 'You're here to win games, and we didn't'
item.dc:creator: BILL TROCCHI
item.description: ATLANTA (AP) — Bryce Harper doesn't play the shoulda, woulda, coulda game. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA (AP) — Bryce Harper doesn't play the shoulda, woulda, coulda game.
The bottom line for the Philadelphia Phillies is they came up short in the postseason again.
“You’re here to do business. You’re here to win games, and we didn’t do that,” Harper said in a subdued Phillies clubhouse Thursday night following their 6-2 loss to the Atlanta Braves in the deciding Game 3 of their National League Wild Card Series.
There would be no excuses coming from the All-Star slugger about a September swoon that prevented the Phillies from lining up their pitching against Atlanta because it took until Game 162 to clinch a playoff spot.
Philadelphia forced Game 3 against the Braves with three dramatic solo home runs late in Game 2. But in the end, the Phillies fell into an early hole Thursday and were eliminated from the postseason for the fifth consecutive year as they chase their first World Series title since 2008.
“You’d love to be able to set your pitching up and them be rested and all that kind of stuff,” interim manager Don Mattingly said. “But that’s not the way it went. We had to fight to get ourselves in, and to do what we had to do to get in, we had to do what we had to do basically every game in the series.”
The Phillies' core of Harper, Kyle Schwarber, J.T. Realmuto, Zack Wheeler and Aaron Nola have made five straight playoff appearances and averaged 91 wins per year during that stretch. They have yet to win a championship and have been eliminated further and further from that goal each season since reaching the 2022 World Series.
The following season, Philadelphia exited in the National League Championship Series, and the next two years saw losses in the Division Series. A wild-card exit this season marks another step in the wrong direction.
“Obviously, we'd love to win a World Series with these guys. We’ve been together quite a while, and we've got a good clubhouse, and you know, good characters on this team,” Nola said. “We know what type of guys are in here. We know what type of players we have, and what we’re capable of. (We need to) kind of play good at the right time.”
The five-year run included two playoff series wins over the Braves. Philadelphia eliminated Atlanta in 2022 and 2023 despite the Braves winning the NL East in both seasons. That scenario was set up again this year, with the Braves earning home-field advantage in this series by virtue of another NL East title.
This time, however, Atlanta managed to get the big hits and the clutch pitching when it mattered most. Ray Kerr, in just his 10th appearance this year and first career postseason appearance, played the role of opener to perfection. He went 3 1/3 innings, giving up no runs, one walk and one hit to set up bulk reliever Grant Holmes.
Michael Harris II belted a three-run homer off Nola in the first, and the Phillies were looking up the rest of the night.
The Phillies were looking up at the rest of their division in April, but eventually righted the ship. Mattingly took over when Rob Thomson was fired on April 28 after a 9-18 start. The Phillies won eight of their next nine and reached .500 on May 16. A red-hot August put them in playoff position, but a postseason berth was not secured until the final game of the regular season.
Mattingly deflected questions about his future after the game.
“It’s not the time to talk about it. I’m comfortable with whatever they want to do,” he said. “Again, I want the best for the Phillies. I loved being in Philly this year. I actually like playing in that environment. I like the environment. It’s a rough environment, but it’s good. Again, I think you let the organization evaluate, talk about what they think moving forward, what they should do, and that dictates a lot of different things.”
As the clubhouse emptied out for the final time this season, Wheeler reflected on the journey the Phillies went on and the disappointing ending it delivered.
“It is tough. We spent a lot of time together. We see everybody’s ups and downs,” he said. “We see the good times and bad times people have throughout the season. We’re all brothers here, and we love to compete. So something like this happens, it’s tough.”

item.title: [nbcphiladelphia.com] Phillies' season ends with the pain of another early postseason knockout
item.dc:creator: Jim Salisbury
item.description: ATLANTA – While the Phillies tried to extend their season Thursday night against the Atlanta Braves at Truist Park, their Delta 757 charter sat 23 miles away at Hartsfield-Jackson International airport. A win would send the Phillies west, to Los Angeles and a second straight National League Division Series matchup with the Dodgers. A loss would send them home, to Philadelphia and another long, cold winter. It didn’t take long to figure out which way the Phillies would be heading. Aaron Nola was
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA – While the Phillies tried to extend their season Thursday night against the Atlanta Braves at Truist Park, their Delta 757 charter sat 23 miles away at Hartsfield-Jackson International airport.
A win would send the Phillies west, to Los Angeles and a second straight National League Division Series matchup with the Dodgers.
A loss would send them home, to Philadelphia and another long, cold winter.
It didn’t take long to figure out which way the Phillies would be heading. Aaron Nola was tagged for three runs in the first inning. The Phillies never recovered. Their season came to an end in a 6-2 loss to the Braves in Game 3 of the NL Wild Card Series.
For just the second time in franchise history, the Phillies qualified for the postseason for a fifth straight year, matching a team-high streak first reached from 2007 to 2011. The Phils won the World Series in 2008, but have not since. They made a surprising run to the World Series in 2022 but were beaten by the Houston Astros in six games. They were a win away from returning to the World Series in 2023 only to collapse and lose Games 6 and 7 of the NL Championship Series at home to Arizona. Since then, they have gone the wrong way, losing in the Division Series (their first round of play) in 2024 and 2025 and now in the Wild Card Series.
“It’s always frustrating,” Kyle Schwarber said in the quiet of the losing clubhouse. “From every postseason I’ve been in, it always hurts when you’re not the last team standing.
“It’s just as frustrating this year as it was last year and the year before that.”
Philadelphia Phillies
Complete coverage of the Fightin' Phils and their MLB rivals from NBC Sports Philadelphia.
As the October defeats have mounted, the team’s core group of high-priced veteran players has gotten older.
Schwarber, always the optimist, insisted that the team’s championship window is still wide open. So did J.T. Realmuto, saying, “There’s definitely the talent in this room to win. If you watched us play all year, no matter who we played, we weren’t outmatched. It’s about execution. It’s not about the age and the years. We know we still have the talent to win.”
Over on the other side of the clubhouse, Bryce Harper didn’t sound so sure.
He was asked what gives him faith that the team can still get to where it wants to go.
“Yeah, I don’t know,” he said. “It’s going to be a long offseason, obviously. I have trust in the organization and the people that are in charge. We’ll see where we go.”
Heading into the offseason, the Phils have many questions, first and foremost: Will Don Mattingly return as manager in 2027? He took over, with an interim tag, for Rob Thomson after the team got off to a 9-19 start in April.
The Phillies played .590 ball (79-55) under Mattingly, but president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski tried to hire Alex Cora when he let Thomson go, and he seems likely to try again in the coming weeks. Stay tuned.
Mattingly would not touch the topic after the game. Schwarber, Realmuto, Nola and Trea Turner all said they’d like to see Mattingly return. Harper declined to talk about the topic.
If Cora comes on board, he will be taking over a team of highs and lows, one with an inconsistent offense that is seemingly up one month (see August) and down the next (see September). He will be taking over a team that lacks pitching depth, both in the starting rotation and the bullpen. Both weaknesses reared their head in recent weeks as the Phils had to scramble to make the playoffs, using ace Zack Wheeler on the final day of the regular season, a circumstance that prevented him from starting Game 1 of the postseason.
Wheeler mentioned the team’s overall inconsistency when asked if he believed the Phils still had the talent to make a deeper postseason run next year.
“Consistency in every group, I think that’s what will get us there,” he said. “We were kind of inconsistent throughout the year. Maybe we were hitting, but we weren’t pitching well. Maybe we were pitching well and we weren’t hitting well. We just have to put it all together throughout the majority of the season.
“We’re hungry, that’s for sure. We just didn’t get the job done.”
The Phils had chances to win the series.
Jesus Luzardo pitched well in Game 1 and they held a 3-2 lead in the seventh. With few trusted arms in his leaky bullpen, Mattingly went to his All-Star closer, Jhoan Duran, in the bottom of the seventh. Duran got through that inning but gave up the lead on a three-run homer in the eighth and the Phillies lost, 5-3.
They bounced back to win a wild Game 2 Wednesday in 10 innings on the strength of three late home runs and the clutch pitching of Cristopher Sanchez, Alex McFarlane and Andrew Painter. They seemed to have momentum heading into Game 3.
But the momentum disappeared quickly as Nola had big trouble throwing strikes.
Just three of the right-hander's first 13 pitches to open the game were strikes. He fell behind Ronald Acuna Jr., and Matt Olson, the Braves’ Nos. 2 and 3 hitters, with 3-0 counts and eventually walked both. He then fell behind Michael Harris II, 2-0. Harris hit the next pitch, a sinker down and out of the zone, over the right-field wall for a three-run homer.
“I think he was just a little too careful,” Realmuto said of Nola. “I don’t think he was way off because he was just missing. They just did a good job of not chasing and making him come in the zone. When a lineup is good like that and they get on a roll, it’s tough to get them out when they’re not chasing.”
Nola did not make it through the second inning. Tim Mayza got the final out of the frame before handing off to Wheeler in the top of the third. The Phillies’ brain trust opted not to start Wheeler on three days’ rest. He'd never done that before. Also, Wheeler admitted that at this point of the season, he wasn’t feeling 100 percent. It was decided that Nola’s best chance of succeeding would be to stay in a starter’s role.
“We’re going to need Nola in this game,” Mattingly said before the game. “Starting him gives us the best version of him.”
The Phillies weren’t sure Wheeler would even be able to pitch until he tested himself by playing catch before the game. He ended up pitching four innings but was not particularly sharp. He gave up three hits and walked three. One of those walks turned into a run when Ozzie Albies stroked a two-run homer in the fourth to give the Braves a 5-0 lead.
“We felt Nola was on solid rest,” Mattingly said after the game. “If he could get us into the game at all, we’d have Zack after that. Obviously, it didn’t go well.”
Atlanta used lefty Ray Kerr as an opener. He pitched 3 1/3 innings and did not allow a run. The only hit Kerr gave up was a single to Schwarber in the first inning. Kerr then struck out Harper.
Grant Holmes, Robert Suarez, Didier Fuentes, Dylan Dodd and Chris Sale finished off the Phillies. Sale, the Braves’ ace lefty who started Game 1, entered with two outs in the eighth and struck out Harper.
Before the 2019 season, Harper signed a 13-year, $330-million contract with the Phillies. He came looking for a parade down Broad Street. Eight years later, he boarded a flight back to Philadelphia, still looking.

item.title: [MLB.com] Kerr, Holmes shine in Braves' Wild Card-clinching win
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman
item.description: ATLANTA -- Ray Kerr was the left-handed reliever the Braves chose to get through Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper during the first inning of Game 3 of the National League Wild Card Series against the Phillies. Kerr served as the opener in Thursday's series-clinching 6-2 win and dazzled, keeping the Phillies in check with 3 1/3 scoreless innings, allowing one hit and one walk with two strikeouts. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Ray Kerr was the left-handed reliever the Braves chose to get through Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper during the first inning of Game 3 of the National League Wild Card Series against the Phillies.
Kerr served as the opener in Thursday's series-clinching 6-2 win and dazzled, keeping the Phillies in check with 3 1/3 scoreless innings, allowing one hit and one walk with two strikeouts. Grant Holmes followed Kerr and allowed one run on two hits and one walk, while earning the win.
“This was just another Thursday,” Kerr said. “Growing up, I had a hard time. So, this was nothing.”
The Braves provided a clue they would go this way in Miami on Friday, when they used Kerr as an opener on Holmes’ scheduled start date.
“That was a best-case scenario, and [Kerr] did it,” Weiss said. “He got through the top twice, which kept us from using another guy at the top. So, Ray -- it all started with Ray. Everything fell into place because of Ray Kerr.”
Kerr posted a 1.47 ERA over 18 1/3 innings in nine appearances going back to his Aug. 17 season debut. Left-handed hitters were 4-for-23 (.174) against him in the regular season, with one extra-base hit, a double.
Kerr made two appearances against the Phillies in September, with the most recent a three-inning outing on Sept. 13. He got Schwarber to ground into a double play and then struck out Trea Turner to end the fifth. Harper began the sixth with a double but was left stranded.
Kerr has made just 19 big league appearances since the start of 2024. After tossing three scoreless innings against the Marlins on Friday, he said he would gladly welcome the chance to be an opener in the postseason.
Holmes posted a 3.57 ERA in 29 starts this season and a 2.94 ERA over his final 14 starts. Opponents produced a .590 OPS against him the first time facing him in a game and an .886 OPS during the second plate appearance.

item.content:encoded:
If you want more Action Network content, be sure to add us as a preferred source on Google.
The Atlanta Braves host the Philadelphia Phillies in Game 3 of their NL Wild Card Series on October 1, 2026. First pitch from Truist Park is scheduled for 8:00 p.m. ET. The game will be broadcast on NBC/Peacock.
The Phillies are favored by -115 on the moneyline and by -1.5 on the run line (+155). The Braves are -105 on the moneyline and +1.5 on the run line (-190). The total is set at 7.5 (+100o / -120u).
Find my Phillies vs Braves prediction for Game 3 below, as well as probable pitchers, starting lineups, the weather forecast and more.
My Phillies vs Braves best bet is on Philadelphia to win outright. Make sure to find the best odds by checking our live MLB odds page, and download the Action Network app for more picks and analysis.
Phillies vs Braves Odds
- Phillies vs Braves moneyline: Phillies -115, Braves -105
- Phillies vs Braves over/under: 7.5 (+100o / -120u)
- Phillies vs Braves spread: Phillies -1.5 (+155), Braves +1.5 (-190)
Phillies vs Braves Preview, Starting Lineups
Phillies Game 3 Lineup
- SS Trea Turner
- 2B Bryson Stott
- LF Bryan De La Cruz
- 3B Edmundo Sosa
- C J.T. Realmuto
- CF Justin Crawford
The best three words in sports are "Win or go home". Everything is on the line here after the Phillies rallied to win Game 2. Their season was on life support until Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hit back-to-back homers to tie the game in the 7th, and Alec Bohm hit the go-ahead homer in the 10th.
The burning question for manager Don Mattingly: Who pitches? Zack Wheeler or Aaron Nola? The answer feels obvious: go with Wheeler, the staff's ace. It would be four days between starts and three days of rest for Wheeler.
Wheeler boasts a 3.00 ERA, a 2.86 xERA, and a 3.35 FIP. He's a strikeout machine, punching out 10.72 per nine, but his walk rate has grown to 2.61 this year. He's rounding into prime form at the best time, pitching to a 1.71 ERA in five September outings.
Diving into the Phillies' pen usage, everything is on the table. The Phillies can add two extra weapons to their pen, with Aaron Nola and Jesus Luzardo as options. Andrew Painter threw 37 pitches in game two — so he might not be an option for Mattingly. The good news? Jhoan Duran will be an option since Painter saved the pen on Wednesday.
Offensively, the Phillies looked rough in the stretch entering the playoffs, but all it takes is one or two long balls to shift this game in their direction.
So far in the Wild Card round, Alec Bohm has been the guy for the Phillies, leading them with a .375 average and a 1.319 OPS. Schwarber and Harper are always a threat, but Bohm playing this well gives Philly a boost.
Braves Game 3 Lineup
- RF Ronald Acuña Jr.
- CF Michael Harris II
- SS Mauricio Dubón
- LF Mike Yastrzemski
- 3B Austin Riley
- 2B Ozzie Albies
- DH Dominic Smith
While the Phillies have multiple strong starter options for a do-or-die Game 3, the Braves have zero rotation depth, and it's showing. The options are a full bullpen game or an opener before Grant Holmes, or Grant Holmes on a short leash.
None of those are ideal options in this spot. The basic stats indicate Holmes had a solid year, posting a 3.44 ERA, but his 5.04 xERA and 4.67 FIP are terrifying in a playoff game. Holmes isn't a swing-and-miss pitcher, striking out just 6.8 hitters per nine innings, and when you can't strike hitters out, they get more chances to do damage.
Holmes also gets hit very hard, ranking in the 1st percentile in average exit velocity and third in hard-hit rate.
In this series, the Braves bats have been more reliable than the Phillies in the middle-to-bottom of the order. However, the top of the order has destroyed them. It starts with Ronald Acuna Jr. with no hits, Drake Baldwin hitting .222, and Matt Olson hitting .125.
Putting it lightly, the Braves will face an uphill battle winning this game if their three best hitters don't hit.
Sure, the Phillies totally limped into the playoffs, but the Braves have some glaring issues of their own, and they're showing up at the worst time. The lineup has been unreliable, and the rotation is a mess.
I want Wheeler or even Nola if he's starting. The Braves have no pitching answers to contain the Philadelphia big boppers.
Take the pitching and road team on the moneyline.
Pick: Phillies ML (-115, BetMGM)

item.title: [MLB.com] What's it like to face Miz? We asked those who have
item.dc:creator: Adam McCalvy; Zach Sweet
item.description: MILWAUKEE -- To the Twins, it looked like a fastball you could see out of the hand – and then it was past you. To the Rockies, it was a pitch that seemed to reach the plate before they could react. The Braves geared up for 100 mph, then found themselves chasing cutters and sliders. The Cubs had faced Jacob Misiorowski more than most teams. Their manager still described a fastball at the top of the strike zone that “nobody can hit.” The Phillies came within one Kyle Schwarber swing of literally g
item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE -- To the Twins, it looked like a fastball you could see out of the hand – and then it was past you. To the Rockies, it was a pitch that seemed to reach the plate before they could react. The Braves geared up for 100 mph, then found themselves chasing cutters and sliders.
The Cubs had faced Jacob Misiorowski more than most teams. Their manager still described a fastball at the top of the strike zone that “nobody can hit.” The Phillies came within one Kyle Schwarber swing of literally getting no hits in nine innings.
“You see some guys that throw 103 [mph], but you get a little bit more time. A guy like that, where he's almost dropping it in the catcher's mitt, man, it makes for a tough day,” Judge said in May, after Misiorowski struck out 11 and touched 103.6 mph in his first career start against the Yankees. “I was excited to get a chance to face him and see him for the first time.
“You know, I’ve seen a lot of his games and seen what he's done; it's impressive stuff, man. They've got a great, great, great young star over there.”
Across the league, opponents spent the season looking for an answer when Misiorowski was on the mound. They struggled, as he finished with a 1.80 ERA, 252 strikeouts, a 0.80 WHIP and a .157 opponents’ average, each the best mark in the Majors. He enters October as the clear favorite for the National League Cy Young Award. On Saturday, the Padres will get the next chance when Misiorowski starts Game 1 of the National League Division Series.
Ask the hitters who faced him what makes the assignment so difficult, and velocity is only the beginning.
“Marshy asked me after the game,” said Phillies star Bryce Harper in June, referring to teammate Brandon Marsh, “he's like, ‘That's probably the best guy I've ever faced.’ And he asked me who’s one of the best guys I've ever faced, and I said Matt Harvey. He had that extension heater, and he was one of the first guys that really rode that heater at the top of the zone. Obviously, 104 [mph] is a little bit different.”
That was after Misiorowski’s finest start of the season, a 15-strikeout, 27-batter, 95-pitch shutout in front of a spellbound crowd at American Family Field on June 12, the one-year anniversary of Misiorowski’s Major League debut.
Harper, perhaps with October in mind, saw a silver lining.
“I'm happy we were able to face him – and I'm not saying that in a good way or bad way, but I was just happy we were able to face him and see what that looked like,” he said.
The Twins had their own trouble in an Aug. 9 matchup, when Misiorowski reached 200 strikeouts faster than all but one pitcher in history. Misiorowski began that night by throwing 21 consecutive four-seam fastballs. Royce Lewis saw one at 103 mph in his first at-bat and called it one of the most difficult pitches he had ever faced.
Brooks Lee noticed how far Misiorowski’s 6-foot-7 frame carried him down the mound, and how his position on the first-base side of the rubber changed the angle. Even a hitter who recognized what was coming had little time to do anything about it.
“It comes out of his hand and you feel like you see it well, and then it’s by you,” Twins hitter Kody Clemens said. “Especially up in the zone.
“If he throws a fastball in the upper part of the zone, I feel like it’s damn near impossible to hit.”
Twins manager Derek Shelton pointed to the pitch’s movement near the top of the zone. Hitters had to judge whether it would be a ball or strike while trying to catch up to 100-plus mph. He called it “probably one of the most challenging at-bats in the game.”
“Honestly, we were scratching, clawing, trying to get to him in any way, shape or form,” Colorado outfielder Cole Carrigg said.
Misiorowski threw 66 pitches at 100 mph or harder that day, a single-game record in the pitch-tracking era. Rockies manager Warren Schaeffer saw more than a radar-gun reading.
“That’s a one-of-one fastball, 103 with all that extension,” Schaeffer said. “It’s hard to react to that. And he throws it all the time.”
Against Atlanta in August, the problem changed shape. Misiorowski threw six scoreless innings in a matchup with Chris Sale, a pitcher he grew up admiring. Sale left impressed by “probably the most impressive fastball I’ve ever seen.” Braves manager Walt Weiss explained what happened when hitters prepared for it.
“You’re gearing up for 100, and then you’re having to deal with cutters and sliders,” Weiss said. “It’s among the toughest at-bats.”
The Cubs’ Seiya Suzuki had offered a similar assessment after facing Misiorowski in June, on the night he fired a 105.5 mph fastball against Pete Crow-Armstrong to match the third-fastest pitch since tracking began in 2008.
“Everybody had good swings and good at-bats,” Suzuki said through interpreter Edwin Stanberry, “but overall, he just pitched better.”
The Cubs did find a way through on Sept. 2 at Wrigley Field, scoring five runs in the first two innings and chasing Misiorowski after four while snapping his streak of 25 consecutive outings allowing three or fewer earned runs. Alex Bregman homered on a slider low in the zone and added a two-run single on a 102 mph fastball. Beforehand, Cubs manager Craig Counsell had identified the opening: Get a pitch lower in the zone, because the high fastball was so hard to hit even when hitters expected it.
“When he executes, you’re in trouble,” Counsell said. “That’s generally how the great ones are.”
Six days later, the Cubs saw him again. Misiorowski opened by striking out Crow-Armstrong on a 103.7 mph fastball, reached 104.5 against Suzuki and allowed one run over 6 1/3 innings. Along the way, he threw his 1,000th pitch of the season at 100 mph or harder.
“That’s how I throw,” Misiorowski said afterward. “The guys on the other side expect that.”
They do. By now, hitters from New York to Philadelphia to Minnesota to Colorado to Atlanta to Chicago, and across the entire league, can describe the fastball, the angle and the pitches that follow.
The Padres will arrive with their own plan. Then someone will have to stand in the box and try to make it work. Nobody has consistently done that against the presumptive NL Cy Young winner in 2026.

Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. item.content:encoded:
What a way to sweep the Red Sox out of the playoffs! The Yankees brushed aside their inferior opponents, winning the two games by a combined score of 18-2. Every facet of their game was clicking — plate discipline, slug, bat-to-ball, two-strike hitting, situational hitting, base running, defense, and of course, starting pitching. It’s a winning recipe that leaves them in good stead for the upcoming ALDS date with Tampa.
The Yankees weren’t the only team to eliminate their opponents from the postseason on Wednesday so let’s jump straight into the action!
AL Wild Card Series Game 2
Chicago White Sox 7, Houston Astros 3
(Chicago wins 2-0)
After just two games, I can’t think of any playoff participant who wants to face these White Sox. That is a sentence that no one could conceive of typing at the start of the season. Two seasons removed from suffering the most losses in MLB history and on the back of three straight losing campaigns, this upstart Chicago squad came out of nowhere to crash the postseason, starting with a two game sweep of the Astros in their own building.
They have done so by scoring early and often, the White Sox lineup a deep unit one-thru-nine with multiple ways to hurt you. They work deep counts, foul pitches off, draw walks, and can put the ball in play, but can also slug the ball out of the yard from almost any spot in the batting order. On Tuesday, they scored three unanswered runs in the first two innings to put the Astros on the back foot from the word go, and Wednesday continued the trend with the Southsiders hanging a four-spot before the home team had a chance to bat.
They had a 1-0 lead just five pitches into the game against Astros ace Hunter Brown, Sam Antonacci leading off with a double before Kyle Teel drove him home with a single. A fielding error by Nick Allen on a Miguel Vargas grounder put a pair on, and three straight singles by Andrew Benintendi, Tristan Peters, and Chase Meidroth plated three more runs with help from a Lucas Spence throwing error from center.
Credit to the Astros, they did not roll over after going down four in the first and slowly chipped into the White Sox lead. Jeremy Peña led off the bottom of the first with a booming home run that clattered off the left field wall just below the train tracks. Cam Smith hit one to almost exactly the same spot with two outs in the second. Jose Altuve narrowly snuck a solo shot into the Crawford Boxes to lead off the fourth and just like that, a 4-0 game had become a 4-3 thriller.
An inning later it looked like the Astros would pull of the improbable and complete the comeback. Smith was hit by a pitch, Peña singled, and Isaac Paredes walked to load the bases with two outs for Altuve. However, reliever Anthony Kay got Altuve to fly out to medium right field to strand all three ducks on the pond. That left the door open for the White Sox to swing the momentum back in their own favor and they did so immediately. Benintendi and Peters drew a pair of walks to open the sixth, prompting Joe Espada to call on Bryan Abreu out of the bullpen. Astros owner Jim Crane vetoed a trade of Abreu to the Twins in the final minutes of the deadline, and Abreu rewarded that faith by hanging a 3-1 slider to Meidroth, the second baseman crushing a three-run bomb to left to put the final nail in the Astros’ coffin.
After sweeping this rematch of the 2005 World Series, the White Sox advance to the ALDS where they will face the AL Central champion Guardians, first pitch of Game 1 scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET on Saturday.
NL Wild Card Series Game 2
Philadelphia Phillies 4, Atlanta Braves 3
(Series tied 1-1)
The Phillies’ season was hanging by a thread until some late heroics by Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper, and Alec Bohm sent this thrilling series to a decisive Game 3. It was a pitchers’ duel early between two starters trending in opposite directions. Tyler Mahle entered his first career playoff start with a sub-two ERA after joining the Braves from the Giants at the deadline while Cristopher Sánchez posted an ERA above five in the month of September (though will still likely wrap up his second straight runner-up finish in NL Cy Young balloting).
The one thing the two starters do have in common is first inning struggles and that certainly played out in this game. Mahle allowed a leadoff double to Trea Turner and consecutive one-out singles by Bryce Harper and Alex Bohm to allow the Phillies to jump ahead, 1-0. However, Sánchez issued a leadoff walk to Ronald Acuña Jr., who promptly stole second and scored the tying run on a Matt Olson single.
Both starters settled in from there, trading zeroes for the next five innings, until things unraveled for Sánchez and his defense in the seventh. Sean Murphy worked a leadoff walk and Ha-Seong Kim reached on a bunt single to put a pair on with no outs. Drake Baldwin then clubbed what looked like a routine liner to right, but Harper misplayed it horrifically breaking in on the ball only to watch it sail over his glove and to the wall for what was ruled as an RBI double. Sánchez intentionally walked Ozzie Albies to load the bases, and Olson made him pay with a sac fly to double the Braves lead, 3-1.
What should have been a hammer blow to the Phillies morale did not play out as such. Schwarber immediately responded with a towering leadoff shot off lefty reliever Dylan Lee, and Harper atoned for his misplay by going back-to-back to retie the game, 3-3. That sent this game to extra innings, where the much-maligned Alec Bohm continued his redemption tour. Bohm was on the bubble of being non-tendered during the offseason, but the Phillies kept him around and drove in the first run of the series with an RBI double in the first inning of Game 1. The third baseman was the ultimate hero in this one, his opposite field solo homer off rookie Didier Fuentes in the 10th to keep the Phillies season alive and force a decisive Game 3.
San Diego Padres 4, Chicago Cubs 1
(San Diego wins 2-0)
This game featured surprisingly quick hooks of both starters as neither manager wanted to risk leaving their highest leverage relievers unused. One was certainly more deserved than the other, Kevin Gausman allowing three runs on five hits in 3.1 innings. The Cubs were desperate for starting pitching at the Trade Deadline and Gausman was supposed to be their big prize. However, he flopped after making the move from the Blue Jays, pitching to a 4.83 ERA in nine starts post-deadline, and his stinker tonight was the beginning of the end of the Cubs’ season. Nick Pivetta on the other hand held Chicago to a run on three hits and two walks with four strikeouts in 3.1 innings, but Craig Stammen seemed determined to play the matchups in this one.
Ty France got things started with a double to lead off the second, advancing to third on a Jackson Merrill single, who then stole second to put a pair in scoring position for Xander Bogaerts. The veteran shortstop opened the scoring with an RBI single, which brought Ethan Salas to the plate. The 20-year-old became the youngest catcher ever to appear in a playoff game, and in his first postseason PA, he lifted a sac fly to center to plate Merrill as the Padres’ second run.
The real story of this series has been the Cubs’ inability to score. They led MLB scoring 5.25 runs per game, spearheaded by shoo-in NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and his MLB-leading 45 home runs (PCA would go 0-for-7 with four strikeouts in the series). They found themselves shut out through the first 12.1 innings of this series, finally breaking the seal in the fourth on a Seiya Suzuki single, Ian Happ walk, and Nico Hoerner RBI single. A Carson Kelly hit-by-pitch loaded the bases with two outs, but Dansby Swanson flew out to stand all three in place.
San Diego immediately punished them for failing to fully cash in on that scoring opportunity. Bogaerts reached on a one-out double, prompting Craig Counsell to call on Daniel Palencia in relief of Gausman. Palencia yanked a 101 mph fastball right into Sheets’ nitro zone down and in, and the lefty crushed it to right for a mammoth two-run blast.
It was all hands on deck from there from the Padres bullpen looking to protect their lead for the final five innings of the contest. They proved how terrifying a relief corps they’ve been all season, allowing just three base runners — a Michael Busch walk with two outs in the fifth, a Tyrone Taylor pinch-hit single with one out in the eighth, and a Hoerner one-out double off Mason Miller in the ninth — after the Cubs stranded the bases loaded to end the fourth.
San Diego advances to the NLDS where they will face the best team in baseball. It’s an unenviable position to come up against presumptive NL Cy Young Jacob Misiorowski and the 103-win Brewers. Game 1 of that series is scheduled for October 3rd with first pitch time contingent upon the result of Game 3 between Philly and Atlanta.

item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Braves will host the Philadelphia Phillies in a decisive Game Three of the National League Wild Card series tonight (Thursday, October 1). The winner will advance to face the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Division Series (NLDS). The Braves won Game One, but the Phillies rallied to win Game Two on Wednesday (September 30), setting the stage for this winner-take-all contest.
The game will start at 8 p.m. ET and will be broadcast on NBC and Peacock. Spanish language coverage will be available on Universo and Univision Radio, while ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB postseason games.
The Phillies' starting pitcher remains undecided, with options including Aaron Nola and ace Zack Wheeler. Meanwhile, the Braves may rely on Grant Holmes to handle the bulk of the innings, though they have not confirmed if he will start or follow an opener. Left-handers Ray Kerr or Brent Suter are potential openers.
Both teams have key players to watch. For the Phillies, Alec Bohm hit a game-winning homer in Game Two, while Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber hit back-to-back homers in the eighth inning to tie the game. On the Braves' side, Michael Harris II and Mauricio Dubón have been performing well at the plate.
The Phillies have a history of postseason success against the Braves, having defeated them in previous playoff series, including the 1993 NLCS and the 2022 and 2023 NLDS. The outcome of tonight's game will determine who advances to face the Dodgers in the next round.
