item.content:encoded:
October baseball is upon us, and we have a massive playoff game on Thursday night.
The Philadelphia Phillies and Atlanta Braves are the only teams remaining in the wild card round, setting up a standalone Game 3 on Thursday night.
The Phillies came back from a 3-1 deficit in Game 2 – after a key Bryce Harper error – to win in extra innings behind solo shots from Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Alec Bohm.
The starting pitching matchup for Game 3 is murky at the moment, although two beat reporters gave some insight into what these teams might do.
Long-time Phillies reporter Jim Salisbury shared that he’s hearing veteran Aaron Nola will get the start for the Phillies while the Braves will go with an opener in Ray Kerr. The Atlanta bullpen is elite, ranking fourth in MLB in ERA during the regular season.
Braves beat reporter Mark Bowman also shared some insight to the starting pitching matchup, mentioning that Braves righty Grant Holmes could be used as the “bulk” option behind Kerr on Thursday. He also believes the Phillies will use a combo of Nola and ace Zack Wheeler, who would be pitching on short rest after leading the Phillies to a win on Sunday.
All hands are going to be on deck in this matchup for both teams, as this is a win-or-go-home scenario.
Oddsmakers have set the Phillies as slight favorites on the road, a sign that they have more confidence in Philly’s options to start in this game.
Here’s a breakdown of the odds, a player prop to bet and my prediction for Thursday’s Game 3.
Phillies vs. Braves Odds, Run Line and Total
Run Line
- Phillies -1.5 (+144)
- Braves +1.5 (-174)
Moneyline
- Phillies: -118
- Braves: -102
Total
- 7.5 (Over +100/Under -120)
Phillies vs. Braves Probable Pitchers
- Philadelphia: TBA
- Atlanta: TBA
Phillies vs. Braves How to Watch
- Date: Thursday, Oct. 1
- Time: 8:00 p.m. EST
- Venue: Truist Park
- How to Watch (TV): NBC, Peacock
- Series: Tied 1-1
Phillies vs. Braves Best MLB Prop bets
Braves Best MLB Prop Bet
- Drake Baldwin OVER 1.5 Hits, Runs, RBIs (-108)
In today’s edition of Walk-Off Wagers – our MLB Best Bets column at SI – I shared why Baldwin is worth a look if Nola gets the start:
If Nola ends up getting the start, it’s a good sign for Braves catcher/designated hitter Drake Baldwin.
Baldwin picked up two hits and a run batted in on Wednesday, and he’s fared extremely well against Nola in his career.
The 25-year-old is 5-for-11 (.455) against Nola in his career, with a .955 OPS. He’s driven in one run against the Phillies veteran, and Nola has struggled quite a bit with the long ball this season, allowing 37 in 33 starts during the regular season.
A homer would immediately hit this prop for Baldwin, and he’s coming off a strong showing on Wednesday. During the regular season, the Braves star hit .284 overall and .307 against right-handed pitching.
Baldwin also entered the playoffs on a hot streak, batting .360 with two home runs, five runs batted in and a .951 OPS over the final two weeks (12 games). He’s a pretty interesting bet with this prop set at -108 on Thursday.
Phillies vs. Braves Prediction and Pick
Another play from today’s Walk-Off Wagers, I’m going to back the Phillies to win and advance after stealing Game 2:
There’s certainly an argument to be made for the Braves, who went 23 games over .500 at home in the regular season, but I lean with the Phillies in Game 3.
If Wheeler is able to pitch on short rest in any capacity, he’ll be by far the best pitcher in this game and had a massive finish to the regular season. Wheeler had a 1.71 ERA in September, lowering his season-long ERA to 3.00. He may not be able to give the Phils a ton of length, but it should help ease the pressure on their bullpen.
Nola has pitched in a ton of big games in his career, and I don’t want to downplay his two solid starts against Atlanta earlier this month. In two outings, Nola allowed just 10 hits and three earned runs across 13.1 innings of work.
The Braves have only used Kerr as an opener once this season, and Holmes had some very shaky advanced numbers in the regular season, ranking in the 12th percentile in expected ERA and the 18th percentile in expected BAA.
The Atlanta bullpen has been taxed in this series, pitching Didier Fuentes, Dylan Lee and Rasiel Iglesias in back-to-back days. That’s not nothing. Can the Atlanta ‘pen hold up after blowing Game 2?
I’d much rather take the Phillies and their proven veteran starters in a winner-take-all game, especially after they showed they can power themselves to a win on Wednesday.
Pick: Phillies Moneyline (-118 at DraftKings)

Just one win, and the Phillies can hop on a flight to Los Angeles to try and get revenge against the Dodgers for last season's NLDS failure. item.content:encoded:
October 01, 2026
It feels sort of unexpected, that the Phillies are not only alive, but have some momentum with the third and final game of the NL Wild Card Series in Atlanta set for Thursday night.
Just one win, and the Phillies can hop on a flight to Los Angeles to try and get revenge against the Dodgers for last season's NLDS failure.
Before Game 3's first pitch, we have a few Phillies' thoughts we'd like to share:
How are we feeling about Aaron Nola — named Game 3's starter earlier Thursday morning? In his 15 starts prior to last Saturday's bizarre three run first inning and out for the Phillies' veteran, Nola boasted a pretty solid 3.12 ERA which is more in line with the Nola who got a monster free agent contract a few offseasons ago.
He's also got some postseason pedigree. He's started 11 playoff games over the last five Octobers, and his two worst starts actually came during the World Series run in 2022. In six starts since 2023, he has a 3.00 ERA and 3-2 record. Is he better than Zack Wheeler pitching on three days rest for the first time ever? The Phils coaching staff made their choice and it's a reasonable one, if nothing else.
If Alec Bohm is parting ways with the Phillies in a few weeks — his contract is set to expire and the Phillies are likely to let him walk and give top prospect Aidan Miller the chance to start the season at third (or second) in 2027 — he gave Phillies fans a spectacular parting gift.
ALEC BOHM GO-AHEAD HOMER
PHILLIES LEAD IN THE 10TH 🤯 pic.twitter.com/S4wFOFyDq1
By virtue of all three other Wild Card series' wrapping up (more on that in a second), the Phillies have Thursday all to themselves and have moved from a 2 p.m. start to prime time (at 8:15 on NBC).
The Phillies are no strangers to primetime playoff starts — they've had a ton of them over the last half decade. They also play better at night. Their win percentage under the lights (55.5%, 61-49) is better than during the afternoon (51%, 26-25). With some extra time for their pitchers to rest and prepare, this is probably a net positive move for the Phillies.
As we just mentioned, the other three series' ended with a 2-0 sweep. Since the league switched to the three-game Wild Card first round format, teams who win Game 1 are now 24-3. The Phillies have a chance to be the fourth.
Philadelphia also has the chance to be the first team in franchise history to win a playoff series (albeit a short one) after losing a Game 1. They are 0-9 historically when they start a series off with a loss.
Another mark, probably, in the Phillies' advantage column is that they're going up against a Braves team unprepared to send a third starter out there. Lefty reliever Ray Kerr — with an impressive 1.77 ERA this season — is going to start the game, likely to face the lefty-heavy front of the Phillies order (Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber). Perhaps the Phillies should consider splitting these hitters up and having Schwarber bat lead off, with Trea Turner second and Harper third?
After Kerr, it's expected the Braves will go to righty starter Grant Holmes, who has a 3.44 ERA this season. Holmes faced the Phillies four times during the regular season and the Phils' hitters will all have recent recollections of facing him.
The Phillies will see how far they can get behind Nola, but it'll be interesting to see who's the next man in. Will it be Jesús Luzardo who pitched in Game 1? Will they ultimately call on Wheeler (or optimistically save him for an NLDS Game 1)? Can Andrew Painter throw on back-to-back days?

item.content:encoded:
Phillies' Aaron Nola Reportedly Starting vs. Braves over Zack Wheeler For MLB Playoffs Series Finale
The Philadelphia Phillies will go into Thursday's winner-take-all Game 3 against the Atlanta Braves in the National League Wild Card series with Aaron Nola starting on the mound.
Per The Athletic's Matt Gelb, Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly is going with Nola rather than using Zack Wheeler on short rest with a spot in the NLDS at stake.
As a result of their four-game losing streak last week that prevented them from clinching a playoff spot early, the Phillies had to use Wheeler on the final day of the regular season.
Wheeler allowed one run over six innings in a 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays to help Philadelphia secure its postseason berth, but the situation left his status for the wild card round unclear.
Even though Wheeler won't get the start, Mattingly told reporters after Wednesday's 4-3 win to extend the series "it'll be pretty much all hands on deck" for Game 3.
The Phillies are fortunate to have a deep starting staff that allowed them to go with All-Stars Jesús Luzardo and Cristopher Sánchez in the first two games against Atlanta.
However, Game 3 left Mattingly with a decision between Nola or Wheeler. John Clark of NBC Sports Philadelphia noted Wheeler has never started a game in the regular season or playoffs on short rest.
Wheeler's only relief appearance in his MLB career was in Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS against the Arizona Diamondbacks. He tossed 1.2 scoreless innings in a 9-7 loss.
Nola will be pitching on regular rest after starting on Saturday against the Rays. He only made it through one inning, allowing three runs on four hits in a 12-1 loss.
While Nola's overall stat line this season doesn't look great with a 4.67 ERA, he did get better as the year went on. The right-hander had a 3.33 ERA in 14 starts after the All-Star break.
Nola made three starts against Atlanta this season with two coming in a five-day span from Sept. 6-11. He allowed three runs and struck out eight over 13.1 innings in those two outings last month.
The Phillies forced Game 3 against Atlanta thanks to Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hitting back-to-back homers in the eighth to tie the score at three. Alec Bohm delivered the go-ahead solo homer in the top of the 10th.
Andrew Painter finished the game on the mound with three scoreless innings out of the bullpen.
Game 3 between the Phillies and Braves from Truist Park will be played at 8 p.m. ET on Thursday. The winner will advance to play the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLDS starting on Saturday.

They wound up losing and hoped that Cristopher Sanchez could get them a Game 2 win to keep the season alive. Thanks to Sanchez, Andrew Painter, Alec Bohm, Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber, the Phillies won Game 2 and will play a Game 3 in a winner-takes-all matchup. But who is going to start for the Phillies? According to Jim Salisbury of NBC Sports Philadelphia, the Phil
item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies sent Jesus Luzardo out to the mound for Game 1 of the NL Wild Card round against the Atlanta Braves. They wound up losing and hoped that Cristopher Sanchez could get them a Game 2 win to keep the season alive.
Thanks to Sanchez, Andrew Painter, Alec Bohm, Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber, the Phillies won Game 2 and will play a Game 3 in a winner-takes-all matchup. But who is going to start for the Phillies?
According to Jim Salisbury of NBC Sports Philadelphia, the Phillies have made their decision between Zack Wheeler and Aaron Nola. The resurgent Nola will get the Game 3 start, as the Phillies hope to clinch Thursday night in Atlanta.
Phillies turn to Aaron Nola for Game 3 vs. Braves
"Hearing Phillies will start Aaron Nola tonight vs. Braves opener Ray Kerr, a lefty," Salisbury reports. "Always subject to change but that's the plan as of this AM."
The Phillies' plan for the winner-takes-all Game 3 of the NL Wild Card series against the Braves will be to start Nola instead of Wheeler on short rest.
While having Wheeler go would've been preferred, if there was ever a time to trust in Nola, it's this season after his second-half resurgence.
As June came to a close, his 6.04 ERA had Phillies fans, rightfully, very concerned about his massive contract going forward.
But his final 11 starts of the 2026 season resulted in an incredible 2.93 ERA. While some luck has gone his way during that stretch, his massive improvement is giving the Phillies enough confidence to turn to him for Game 3.
On the other side, the Braves are reportedly going to start Ray Kerr, a left-handed pitcher, as potentially an opener until they turn the reins over to Grant Holmes.
The Phillies have Wheeler as an option out of the bullpen for multiple innings in Game 3, but ideally they'll ride Nola for as long as possible.
If they could somehow win without pitching Wheeler, that would be the best-case scenario. The same goes for both Jesus Luzardo and Andrew Painter, both of whom would be willing to pitch in Game 3 if needed.
With how shaky the bullpen is, the Phillies are really going to need Nola to go deep into this game, unless the Phillies' offense comes alive and blows this game out of proportion, and some normal relievers can come into the game without worry of blowing it.
But the most important thing is how Nola performs, as he's expected to get the ball to start the game. It's the right call, especially considering how he's on normal rest and is more ready to go than any other pitcher on the roster.

item.content:encoded:
PHILADELPHIA -- Philadelphia Phillies star Bryce Harper said Monday that he did not know how FanDuel would use a personalized video he made for a customer, who has since accused the sportsbook in a lawsuit of taking advantage of his gambling addiction.
In a statement posted on Instagram, Harper said he would not have made the video if he had known FanDuel's intent to use it as part of a VIP promotion or the betting habits of the customer, Terry Thompson.
"I did not know FanDuel would do this," Harper wrote. "I did not consent to it, and FanDuel had no right to do it."
Harper said he received a request on Cameo in November 2024 to read the provided script for a personal "holiday video for Terry." The Philadelphia Inquirer published portions of the video in a story last Thursday, and Harper included a screenshot of the Cameo request with his statement.
"Hey, Terry? What's up, brother? Hey, man, your host Bryttanni from FanDuel wanted to make sure your Thanksgiving was extra special," Harper says in the opening of the video.
Thompson in March sued FanDuel and his VIP host Bryttanni Morgan, along with DraftKings, the NFL and the league's official data distributor, Genius Sports, claiming that the sportsbooks caused him to become addicted, leading to approximately $2 million in betting losses.
"Had I known FanDuel's true intent, I would not have made the video," Harper said. "The same is true had I known anything about Terry or his situation, or about any alleged 'partnership' between Cameo and FanDuel."
The suit alleges that Morgan contacted Thompson with promotional offers and gifts to encourage him to wager more on FanDuel, including tickets and hotel accommodations to attend the Super Bowl.
Major League Baseball's collective bargaining agreement allows players to do promotions with sportsbooks as long as they do not authorize the use of their name, uniform number, image or likeness, or promote betting on baseball.
FanDuel referred ESPN to its previous statement on the Harper issue, stating that its employees "are trained to recognize and flag signs of problem gambling and offer resources and tools."
"We continue to review and strengthen our policies to ensure we have the industry's strongest consumer protection initiatives," the statement read.
Major League Baseball and the MLBPA declined comment on Harper's statement.
A spokesperson for the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board told ESPN that it is reviewing the matter.

item.dc:creator: Redacción OnCuba

item.content:encoded:
La segunda jornada de la Serie de Comodín en la temporada de las Grandes Ligas (MLB, por sus siglas en inglés) selló el adiós de los dos cubanos más mediáticos de la Liga Americana: el slugger Yordan Álvarez y el lanzador Aroldis Chapman.
Los Astros de Houston, de los que Yordan fue bujía a lo largo de la campaña, cayeron en apenas dos juegos ante los Medias Blancas de Chicago, mientras a los Medias Rojas de Chapman los frenaron en seco uno de los exequipos del cerrador holguinero: los Yankees en Nueva York.
Los Medias Blancas ganaron este miércoles 7-3 en Houston y completaron la barrida sobre los Astros. Así, dejaron sin opciones al tunero de seguir ensanchando la mejor campaña de su trayectoria, coronada con el liderazgo de bateo del circuito con promedio de .316, además de despachar 42 jonrones y luchar por la Triple Corona hasta el final del calendario regular.
Houston, we don’t have a problem pic.twitter.com/NmPM6SCndJ
— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) October 1, 2026
Poco pudo aportar Yordan a la causa, al irse en blanco en cuatro visitas al plato. Con ello dejó su producción ofensiva en la postemporada en solo un imparable en los ocho turnos oficiales sumados por él en los dos choques disputados.
La suerte estuvo siempre del lado visitante, pues Chicago anotó cuatro veces en el primer episodio ante el abridor Hunter Brown, ayudado por errores defensivos. En lo adelante, los Astros solo pudieron responder con jonrones solitarios de José Altuve, Jeremy Peña y Cam Smith.
Este duelo era el de mayores expectativas entre los aficionados cubanos dada la presencia en el bando de Chicago del joven antesalista Miguel Vargas, quien tuvo su mejor temporada en la fase preliminar, pero no ha tenido un feliz estreno en la instancia decisiva.
El habanero volvió a fallar en cinco turnos, lo que, unido a un similar desempeño en el choque anterior, lo mantiene a la espera de su primer imparable en la postemporada.
Esta vez el protagonismo recayó en Chase Meidroth, autor de un vuelacercas de tres carreras, y en el bullpen encabezado por Erick Fedde y Jordan Hicks, quienes no permitieron hits en cuatro entradas combinadas para apuntalar la victoria de Anthony Kay.
3-RUN POSTSEASON HOMER FOR CHASE MEIDROTH! pic.twitter.com/39yNEWjiLt
— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) September 30, 2026
Boston desarmado
En el Yankee Stadium, los dueños de casa complacieron a sus parciales con la segunda victoria seguida ante los Medias Rojas de Boston, esta por 9-2. El éxito dejó sin opciones de supervivencia a sus archienemigos históricos y marcó el cierre de temporada para su cerrador estrella Aroldis Chapman.
Max Fried trabajó seis entradas, con seis ponches y una carrera limpia, y fue respaldado por Cody Bellinger al conectar jonrón y producir cuatro anotaciones.
CODY BELLINGER THREE-RUN HOMER
IT’S 8-1 YANKEES! pic.twitter.com/gUQC8CJQb9
— MLB (@MLB) October 1, 2026
Luis García Jr. también firmó un significativo aporte al batear de 5-3 con otro vuelacercas, signo de la oportunidad de los bateadores del Bronx, quienes ligaron de 9-6 con corredores en posición de anotar.
Sonny Gray cargó con la derrota, que tampoco pudieron evitar varios relevistas, entre ellos Garrett Crochet y Garrett Whitlock.
Chapman, sin oportunidad de cerrar un juego ajustado en la serie de comodín, tuvo una entrada de actuación en la que ponchó a los tres bateadores que enfrentó.
Con ese despliegue se convirtió en el primer jugador nacido en Cuba con participación en 10 postemporadas de MLB, y en el segundo de Latinoamérica con 10 o más experiencias de este tipo, solo superado por el legendario panameño Mariano Rivera (16).
¡EL MISIL SIGUE HACIENDO HISTORIA! 🇨🇺
Aroldis Chapman se convierte en el 2do jugador nacido en Latinoamérica en participar en 10 diferentes #Postseason uniéndose a Mariano Rivera. pic.twitter.com/1VjtJcLAZO
— MLB Español (@mlbespanol) October 1, 2026
Además, con los tres ponches recetados llegó a 76 ponches en octubre, para colocarse en el listado histórico de relevistas por detrás de Rivera (110) y Kenley Jansen (94).
Con 38 años, el holguinero cerró una de sus mejores experiencias de las últimas temporadas. A lo largo del tramo regular fijó una efectividad de 1.92 carreras limpias por juego, con 35 salvamentos y 71 ponches en 51.2 entradas.
Sin Cachorros en juego
Las cosas también fueron bien en casa para los Padres de San Diego, al despachar por segunda ocasión sucesiva a los Cachorros de Chicago, esta vez con pizarra de 4-1.
Gavin Sheets conectó jonrón de dos carreras, al tiempo que Xander Bogaerts y Ty France aportaban dos hits cada uno.
Summer’s over, we’re on to October. pic.twitter.com/I4KRWqSyyf
— San Diego Padres (@Padres) October 1, 2026
La ocasión fue propicia para que el relevista cubano Adrián Morejón debutara en la serie lanzando dos entradas en blanco, con un hit permitido, sirviendo de puente hacia los cerrojos de Mason Miller y Jason Adam.
Todo lo contrario sucedió en Atlanta, donde los Filis de Filadelfia lograron equilibrar el pulso con una victoria 4-3 sellada en 10 entradas, que extendió hasta este jueves la definición del trámite.
Kyle Schwarber, Bryce Harper y Alec Bohm combinaron su poder con jonrones para la causa de los visitantes, mientras que el joven Andrew Painter retiraba a los bateadores de Atlanta durante tres entradas en blanco para quedarse con la victoria.
Well, that was wild pic.twitter.com/FpU4KdGxXo
— Philadelphia Phillies (@Phillies) September 30, 2026
El relevista cubano Raisel Iglesias trabajó un inning por los Bravos, con un hit permitido y sin tolerar carreras.
A la espera de esta decisión, los Medias Blancas se alistan para enfrentar a los Guardianes de Cleveland en la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana, que arranca el venidero sábado 3 de octubre.
Por su parte, los Yankees enfrentarán con el mismo objetivo a los Rays de Tampa Bay, que cuentan en su filas con los cubanos con el cubano Yandy Díaz y Victor Mesa Jr.
En la Liga Nacional, San Diego pactó su choque con los Cerveceros de Milwaukee —el mejor equipo de la temporada regular con 103 victorias— y los actuales campeones, los Dodgers de Los Ángeles, con el cubano Andy Pagés entre sus referentes, aguardan para conocer su primer rival en la ruta hacia la conquista de su tercera Serie Mundial consecutiva.

item.title: [MLB.com] Phillies vs. Braves NL Wild Card Series Game 3 FAQ (8 ET, NBC/Peacock)
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman; Todd Zolecki; Paul Casella
item.description: In a series that is shaping up to be another instant classic between the bitter NL East rivals, it now all comes down to Game 3 on Thursday. A Phillies win would set up an NLDS rematch from last year against the Dodgers, while the Braves hope to punch their ticket to the NLDS for the first time since 2023. “Just win a game,” said Phillies infielder Alec Bohm, who hit the game-winning homer in the Phillies’ 4-3 extra-inning victory in Game 2. “ … I think as much as we want to enjoy this for a lit
item.content:encoded:
In a series that is shaping up to be another instant classic between the bitter NL East rivals, it now all comes down to Game 3 on Thursday. A Phillies win would set up an NLDS rematch from last year against the Dodgers, while the Braves hope to punch their ticket to the NLDS for the first time since 2023.
“Just win a game,” said Phillies infielder Alec Bohm, who hit the game-winning homer in the Phillies’ 4-3 extra-inning victory in Game 2. “ … I think as much as we want to enjoy this for a little bit, it's the same as we did [after Game 1]: Turn the page, and move on to tomorrow and show up ready to do the same thing.”
So, what could the Phillies and Braves possibly have in store for their winner-take-all showdown?
While that’s the biggest question looming over the National League Wild Card Series, it’s far from the only one. Here’s everything you need to know about Game 3:
When is the game and how can I watch it?
The game will begin at 8 p.m. ET and air on NBC and Peacock.
The Wild Card Series will be available in Spanish on Universo, while Univision Radio will provide Spanish language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB postseason games, beginning with the Wild Card Series.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Phillies: TBD
The Phillies planned to meet following Game 2 to discuss their pitching plans for this week’s third elimination game. Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said Monday that Aaron Nola was setting up to start Game 3, but there’s no question things can change. It wouldn’t be a surprise to see ace Zack Wheeler start on short rest. If he doesn’t start, there’s no doubt he’d enter the game in relief.
Braves: TBD
Grant Holmes will attempt to handle the bulk of the innings. But the Braves haven’t said whether he’ll start or possibly follow an opener. The top options to open are left-handers Ray Kerr or Brent Suter. Either would be tasked with handling Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber in the first inning.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Braves: The Braves’ lineup appears much more formidable against right-handed pitchers. With Mike Yastrzemski in left field, Mauricio Dubón would move to shortstop, which was where Ha-Seong Kim started during the first two games.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Phillies: Mattingly said it’s “all hands on deck,” although closer Jhoan Duran wasn’t available in Game 2. Mattingly said he hoped he’d have Duran in Game 3. But other than Cristopher Sánchez, who started Game 2, probably every pitcher on the Phillies’ staff will be available in some capacity in Game 3. That’s everybody from Wheeler to Luzardo to Painter.
Braves: Closer Raisel Iglesias and his top setup men Didier Fuentes and Dylan Lee both pitched in the first two games of this series. Each should be available in this winner-take-all game. Robert Suarez hasn’t been utilized yet. He missed three months with an elbow ailment before making two appearances last week. But manager Walt Weiss may have no other choice but to turn to the right-hander, who posted a 0.56 ERA in 31 appearances before his elbow became a problem in June.
Any injuries of note?
Braves: OF Lane Thomas could be available during the NLDS. Starting pitchers Bryce Elder (arthroscopic knee surgery), Reynaldo López (right shoulder inflammation) and Martín Pérez (lower back discomfort) may also be available in future rounds.
Who is hot and who is not?
Phillies: Home runs often come in bunches for Schwarber and Harper. Did their back-to-back homers in the eighth inning in Game 2 get them going? Bohm is 3-for-8 with one double and one home run in the series. After struggling all season, Realmuto has two hits and two RBIs this series.
Anything else fans might want to know?
The Phillies are 1-3 in franchise history in win-or-go-home postseason games. They won Game 5 of the 1980 NLCS. They lost Game 7 of the 2023 NLCS, Game 5 of the 2011 NLDS and Game 5 of the 1981 NLDS.

item.content:encoded:
Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series was deadlocked at 3-3 Wednesday afternoon before Alec Bohm delivered Philadelphia’s biggest swing. His two-out homer in the 10th inning lifted the Phillies to a 4-3 victory over the Atlanta Braves and forced a winner-take-all Game 3.
The Phillies had trailed 3-1 before Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hit back-to-back homers in the seventh. Harper’s blast came one inning after he committed a costly fielding error.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
Andrew Painter then took over. The regular-season starter worked three scoreless innings to protect Philadelphia’s taxed bullpen, stranded two runners in the 10th and struck out Dominic Smith after the Phillies won an ABS challenge.
Playing under traditional extra-inning rules that don’t include designated runners at second base like in the regular season, Bohm delivered his third career postseason home run, a 357-foot shot to right field off right-hander Didier Fuentes.
The Phillies will try to continue their postseason dominance over the Braves in Thursday’s Game 3. Philadelphia beat Atlanta in the 1993 NLCS and the 2022 and 2023 NLDS.
In the seventh, Drake Baldwin’s double glanced off Harper’s glove in right field, driving in Sean Murphy to give Atlanta a 2-1 lead. Harper, who resumed playing the outfield late this season for the first time since 2022, got a poor jump and was leaping for the ball near the warning track. He was not charged with an error. Matt Olson added a sacrifice fly.
“Probably should have been caught, obviously,” Harper said.
The Phillies pulled even with eighth-inning home runs by Schwarber and Harper off Dylan Lee, the winning pitcher in the Braves‘ 5-3 opening win on Tuesday. Schwarber’s drive carried 447 feet and Harper followed with a 418-foot drive.
Tyler Mahle allowed one run on six hits in seven innings for Atlanta. Cristopher Sánchez allowed three runs in 6 2/3 innings for Philadelphia while throwing a career-high 116 pitches.

Tyler Mahle allowed one run on six hits in seven innings for Atlanta. Cristopher Sánchez allowed three runs in 6.2 innings for Philadelphia while throwing a career-high 116 pitches.
The start time for the decisive Game 3 has not yet been determined. The Braves announced that MLB will schedule the game for either 2:15 p.m. ET or 8:15 p.m. ET in Atlanta, with the final time dependent on the conclusion of the other three Wild Card Series Game 2 matchups tonight.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: [MLB.com] Bullpen stung by long ball after Mahle's strong playoff debut
item.dc:creator: Mark Bowman
item.description: ATLANTA -- Six outs away from finally killing Philadelphia’s hex, the Braves were undone by their bullpen, the portion of their roster that was supposed to be a postseason strength. “I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers of all time,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA -- Six outs away from finally killing Philadelphia’s hex, the Braves were undone by their bullpen, the portion of their roster that was supposed to be a postseason strength.
“I was at shortstop when Kirk Gibson did his thing off one of the greatest closers of all time,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said. “It comes with the territory when you're pitching late in close games. Every once in a while, they get you.”
Nearly 40 years later, Weiss still remembers the sting he and his A’s teammates felt when an injured Gibson came off the bench to hit a walk-off homer against Hall of Fame closer Dennis Eckersley in Game 1 of the 1988 World Series at Dodger Stadium.
A similar type of sting was felt as the Braves blew a two-run eighth-inning lead in a 4-3, 10-inning loss to the Phillies in Game 2 of the NL Wild Card Series on Wednesday afternoon at Truist Park. Dylan Lee surrendered consecutive homers to Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper in the eighth. Didier Fuentes allowed Alec Bohm’s decisive homer with two outs in the 10th.
“That's life,” Braves starting pitcher Tyler Mahle said. “Sometimes, it happens. There's nothing really else to say about it. It sucks now, but we're going to have a chance to go out there tomorrow and turn it around.”
Now, Weiss’ bunch must win Game 3 on Thursday to avoid being eliminated from the playoffs by Philadelphia for the fourth time overall and third time in the past five years. The Phillies eliminated Atlanta teams that won 100-plus regular-season games in 1993 (NLCS), 2022 (NLDS) and 2023 (NLDS).
Thursday's Game 3, airing on NBC and Peacock, will start at 8 p.m. ET.
“[The Braves] have played great at home,” Harper said. “But again, I'll just talk about the postseason; it's just a different animal.”
Mahle proved he was up to the challenge during what was his first postseason appearance. The right-hander, acquired from the Giants on Aug. 2, became the first Braves pitcher to allow one run or none over seven-plus innings in the postseason since Max Fried threw seven scoreless against the Reds in Game 1 of the 2020 NL Wild Card Series.
Once Harper misplayed a Drake Baldwin fly ball into a go-ahead double off Phillies starter Cristopher Sánchez during Atlanta’s two-run seventh, it looked like the Braves were destined for a great storyline.
But instead of celebrating how their trade acquisition helped them end the Phillies’ playoff dominance, the Braves were reminded that Lee hasn’t been nearly as good as he was before the All-Star break, when he posted a 1.47 ERA in 43 innings (44 appearances).
When Schwarber opened the eighth with a Statcast-projected 447-foot homer and Harper followed by depositing another ball into the right-field seats, Lee extended the troubles he had while posting a 6.00 ERA in 24 innings after the break. It should be noted he allowed just two homers during that stretch, and he did not allow any home runs to left-handed batters during the regular season.
“Lee’s our high-leverage lefty,” Weiss said. “He put down the same part of the order yesterday.”
Lee struck out Schwarber and got Harper to fly out in Game 1. How might he fare if he’s asked to go through these left-handed sluggers for a third straight day?
How about Fuentes? The rookie right-hander was masterful during the regular season, posting a 2.05 ERA in 70 1/3 innings as a reliever. But he surrendered J.T. Realmuto’s two-run triple in Game 1, and his psyche was bruised again Wednesday when Bohm sneaked his game-winning homer over the right-field wall.
“[Fuentes] made a good pitch,” Baldwin said. “I think if we need him tomorrow, he'll be ready to go, and I don't think he'll let that affect him too much.”
The Phillies’ rotation was a concern entering this series because Zack Wheeler was needed to pitch on Sunday with a postseason spot on the line. Well, Aaron Nola and Wheeler could be used in Game 3.
As for the Braves, they haven’t announced who will start Game 3. Grant Holmes will be lined up to pitch at least four innings. But will he start? Or will either Ray Kerr or Brent Suter take the mound as an opener?
More importantly, can the Braves bounce back from this and finally end their playoff struggles against their division rivals?

item.content:encoded:
Bryce Harper Reacts to Game-Tying HR After Misplay in Phillies Win vs. Braves in MLB Playoffs G2
Philadelphia Phillies star Bryce Harper had quite the sequence between the bottom of the seventh inning and the top of the eighth during his team's 4-3 win Wednesday
A costly fielding error ultimately led to a pair of Braves' runs, allowing them to take a 3-1 lead. But Harper then followed up Kyle Schwarber's solo homer with one of his own the very next inning, tying the game right back up.
Harper spoke about both moments following the win:
"You've got to flush [the mistake] as quickly as possible knowing that [Braves' pitcher Dylan Lee] is coming into the game," Harper said. "And obviously I was hearing it pretty good from Braves' and Phillies' fans behind the dugout. So gotta show up in that situation. Kyle had a great at-bat and then... I wasn't not trying to hit a homer, I'll tell you that."
Harper primarily played first base this season and shifted to right field after second baseman Luis Arráez—who is unavailable for this series due to a sprained ankle suffered last Thursday—was acquired at the trade deadline, requiring a reshuffling of the infield. He's generally been steady since moving back to the outfield, though Wednesday's error was nearly costly.
And his redemption arc wasn't complete without a few of his teammates chipping in.
There was pitcher Andrew Painter, who came out of the bullpen and threw three scoreless innings, earning the win. Not too shabby for Philadelphia's fifth starter, who isn't accustomed to pitching out of the bullpen.
Or as Harper described Painter's performance: "Absolute dawg mentality, closes the door for us."
And then there was Alec Bohm, who put the Phillies up by a run in the top of the 10th inning with an opposite-field homer.
"No, I didn't," Bohm admitted in his post-game interview on NBC when asked if he knew he hit a homer off the bat. "I don't really know what happened. I was trying to pull the ball off the foul pole and I hit it to right field so, I'll take it."

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Bryce Harper lets Braves take lead with fielding blunder, makes up for it with game-tying HR next inning

item.content:encoded:
This was quite a sequence for Bryce Harper.
With his Philadelphia Phillies facing elimination Wednesday against the Braves, the two-time MVP made a critical, late-game defensive blunder that allowed Atlanta to take the lead.
With two men on and one out in a 1-1 game in the bottom of the seventh, Braves slugger Drake Baldwin hit a deep fly ball to right field. Harper was in position to make the catch, but he misjudged the ball.
By the time he realized his mistake, it was too late. He backed up toward the warning track, but the ball bounced off his glove and over his head. The misplay allowed Sean Murphy to score from second for a 2-1 Atlanta lead.
The play was ruled a double, but it was clearly a mistake on Harper's part — one that he admitted in a postgame on-field interview with NBC. The Braves went on to take a 3-1 lead before the frame was done.
But given the chance, Harper immediately made up for his miscue at the plate.
Harper's teammate Kyle Schwarber led off the top of the eighth inning with a solo home run to cut Atlanta's lead to 3-2. One batter later, Harper followed with his own solo blast off Dylan Lee to tie the game 3-3.
The Phillies ultimately won 4-3 in the 10th after an Alec Bohm homer gave them the advantage in the top of the frame. They'll play a deciding Game 3 vs. the Braves on Thursday in Atlanta.
Harper has spent most of his career on defense in the outfield, but he has played primarily at first base or designated hitter since undergoing Tommy John surgery in 2022. When the Phillies traded for infielder Luis Arráez at the trade deadline this summer, Harper moved back to right field.
On Wednesday, it looked like he wasn't quite comfortable in that spot. But Harper has never been uncomfortable with the bat in his hand.

item.content:encoded:
The duality of Bryce Harper was on full display Wednesday afternoon in Atlanta.
In the span of six batters in the seventh inning, Harper badly misplayed a ball in right field that allowed the go-ahead run to cross the plate and hit a game-tying home run as part of back-to-back homers with Kyle Schwarber. Harper also drove in the game's first run with a single in the first inning. He went 2 for 5 in the Phillies' Game 2 win (PHI 4, ATL 3 in 10 innings).
"Schwarb, Harp, after we give up those two, they got momentum," Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said. "And to be able to get that back right away was huge."
Philadelphia rearranged its defense to accommodate Luis Arraez at the trade deadline, which pushed Alec Bohm from third base to first base and Harper from first base back to right field. The results were not always positive. On Wednesday, Bohm failed to get an out on a bunt in that seventh inning immediately prior to Harper's misplay. Drake Baldwin lifted a fly ball that Harper misplayed into a double, which gave the Phillies a 2-1 lead.
"Obviously a world of emotion there," Harper said of his misplay. "I didn't think he hit it very hard and I realized he only hit 89 (mph exit velocity), so I thought it was going to be a pop fly just right at me and then it kind of kept traveling. Obviously a ball I should have caught."
Based on the exit velocity and launch angle, Statcast registered Baldwin's double -- "double" -- with an .080 expected batting average. Stats aside, it's a ball that must be caught, much like Ha-Seong Kim's bunt was a ball that had to be turned into an out. Bohm hesitated just enough for Sean Murphy to beat the throw to second base. Little things that cost the Phillies.
"I think it's a ball Bryce probably thinks he should have caught," Mattingly said. "It looked like it kept carrying a little bit. But no, you don't need to say anything to guys like that in that spot, not in this moment."
Matt Olson followed Baldwin's double -- again, "double" -- with a sacrifice fly to give the Braves a 3-1 lead in the seventh inning. The two misplays contributed directly to the two runs. Harper redeemed himself, though. He and Schwarber hit the back-to-back homers in the next half-inning to tie the game 3-3.
Those were the first two home runs Braves setup man Dylan Lee gave up to left-handed batters this season.
"Lee is our high-leverage lefty," Braves manager Walt Weiss said. "Put down the same part of the order yesterday pretty easily. Threw the ball really well yesterday. That's his inning every time."
Bohm redeemed himself as well. After botching the bunt, he hit a go-ahead home run in the top of the tenth inning, which stood up as the game-winning run thanks to Andrew Painter's heroic three-inning relief appearance. The Phillies have pulled even with the Braves in the Wild Card Series. The decisive Game 3 will be played Thursday afternoon.
"There's been a lot of ups and downs," Bohm said about his season. "Didn't start the best. I don't really know how to put it all into words quickly, but it's just been a long road with a lot of ups and downs. I've learned a lot, and I've made a lot of really close friends along the way and had a lot of people to lean on along the way. I really wouldn't have rather had it any other way."
To make the infield work with Arraez, the Phillies shifted Bryson Stott from second base to third, Bohm from third base to first, and Harper from first base to right. Prior to Arraez's arrival, Harper had not played the outfield since 2022. He moved to first base that summer to limit his throwing following his return from Tommy John surgery.
Arraez rolled his ankle at the end of the regular season and is not on the Wild Card Series roster. His status for the rest of the postseason, should the Phillies advance, is up in the air.

Philadelphia Phillies right fielder Bryce Harper made a crucial mistake in Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series against the Atlanta Braves at Truist Park.
With runners on first and second base and one out in the bottom of the seventh inning, Braves DH Drake Baldwin hit a deep fly ball to right field. Harper misplayed the ball, allowing Baldwin to reach on a double and a run to score, giving Atlanta a 2-1 lead.
The Braves added another run in the inning on a sacrifice fly from Matt Olson.
If the Phillies lose today, they will be eliminated from the postseason. If they come back, there will be a Game 3 tomorrow.

item.content:encoded:
It’s do or die for the Phillies on Wednesday.
The Braves pushed them to the brink in Game 1 of the National League Wild Card with a 5-3 decision prompted by Austin Riley’s three-run shot in the eighth inning.
Another win in this series would mark first time the Braves prevailed over their NL East rivals in the postseason: the Phillies took the NLDS in both 2022 and 2023 and the 1993 NLCS over Atlanta.
This Phillies’ core has been chasing after a World Series throughout the decade, and another early exit will have its ramifications.
The onus to avoid that comes down to no one more than Bryce Harper, who struck out twice and went hitless Tuesday.
Phillies vs. Braves Game 2 prediction, best bet
Harper, who is a .269 postseason hitter in 58 games, narrowly missed a go-ahead two-run home run against Chris Sale in the sixth inning when the ball just sailed just right of the right-field pole.
He gets the lefty vs. righty matchup advantage against Atlanta’s Tyler Mahle, against whom he has posted a healthy .278/.350/.500 slash line.
Mahle leans on his four-seamer for nearly half of his pitches. He doesn’t throw it with extreme movement or overpowering velocity, averaging 92 mph, but he locates the strike zone with it well.
In the 14 four-seamers that Mahle served to Harper this season, Harper knocked two hits with a home run on eight swings, according to Statcast. Only two were whiffs.
In fact, Mahle wasn’t much of a swing-and-miss pitcher at all, ranking in only the 31 percentile.
That’s all while Harper remained an elite contact hitter, posting a .379 xwOBA, a Statcast metric that measures expected offensive production based on the exit velocity and launch angle of his contact rather than the results.
Harper has stated he loves playing at Truist Park, and his numbers say why.

The two-time MVP hit .320 there in 27 plate appearances this season, which included a pair of home runs and five multi-base games out of six.
As the clubhouse leader, Harper was adamant about how the Phillies need to “finish the job” this postseason after having been here before.
He’ll have no choice but to deliver on that statement Wednesday.

item.title: [si.com] MLB Postseason Power Rankings: Strength and Weaknesses for Every Playoff Team
item.dc:creator: Karl Rasmussen
item.description: The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series. The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. Meanwhile, the final domino to fall in the American League went in favor of the Astros, who secured the AL West title with a victory over the Athletics on Sunday. Houston becomes the worst team
item.content:encoded:
The postseason field is finally set. After Sunday’s results on the final day of the regular season, we officially know what 12 teams will be in contention for the 2026 World Series.
The Diamondbacks, despite their late push, fell short of the playoffs, thanks to a Phillies win on Sunday against the Rays. Meanwhile, the final domino to fall in the American League went in favor of the Astros, who secured the AL West title with a victory over the Athletics on Sunday. Houston becomes the worst team to ever make the playoffs in a 162-game season, sneaking in and winning the division with just an 81–81 record.
Fans won’t have to wait long for postseason to get underway, with the Wild Card series set to begin on Tuesday. But before the action gets going, we’re going to do a final power ranking, assessing where all 12 teams sit and detailing their biggest strength and weakness.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching, lineup
Biggest weakness: Bullpen
The Dodgers may be the No. 2 seed in the National League, but they’re built to win in October. It’s hard to determine what’s a greater strength between their loaded starting rotation or their star-studded lineup. There’s no weaknesses in their rotation, with All-Star caliber pitchers available to take the mound every night, even with Shohei Ohtani restricted to DH duties. There isn’t a team in MLB with more postseason experience than Los Angeles, who have won back-to-back World Series with this core. During the regular season, the Dodgers had MLB’s second-highest OPS (.762) and fourth-best ERA (3.55). If there’s any way to beat them it’s by getting after a bullpen that has been inconsistent throughout the season, though it’s still a top-10 unit. Injuries have plagued their relief pitching corps, however, with the likes of Blake Treinen, Edgardo Henriquez and Will Klein all currently on IL.
2. Milwaukee Brewers
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Brewers’ rotation, headlined by NL Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski, has been one of MLB’s best, and it’s helped the team secure the league’s best regular-season record. The starting rotation owns MLB’s fifth-best ERA (3.65) and their bullpen has been equally impressive, ranking third in MLB with a 3.40 ERA. Milwaukee has scored the second-most runs in the league this season (832), as their small-ball approach has worked wonders for them. But in October, when a single swing of the bat can dramatically change a team’s fortunes and rallies are harder to come by, they might not have the power hitters capable of providing that big home run swing. The Brewers didn’t have a single 30-home run hitter this season and had just three everyday starters with a slugging percentage above .450.
3. Tampa Bay Rays
Biggest strength: Elite starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Bottom-third of the lineup
The Rays had the best record in the American League this season, largely thanks to their pitching. The starting rotation has been excellent, ranking third in MLB with a 3.51 ERA. Drew Rasmussen has quietly been one of MLB’s best arms, and Freddy Peralta has begun to rediscover his previous form after a rough go with the Mets and a shaky start on the mound in Tampa. Much like the Brewers, the Rays primarily utilize a small-ball approach offensively. The Rays hit the ninth-fewest home runs in MLB this year, and despite rostering some elite hitters such as Junior Caminero and Yandy Diaz, they haven’t received much production out of the bottom third of their lineup, which is their biggest weakness with the postseason looming.
4. Atlanta Braves
Biggest strength: Deep lineup
Biggest weakness: Plate discipline, low on-base rates
The Braves are another team with an abundance of postseason experience in the lineup. They have several players that can turn a game on its head with one swing of the bat, and had five 20-plus home run hitters during the regular season in Matt Olson, Michael Harris, Drake Baldwin, Ozzie Albies and Ronald Acuña Jr. Although the lineup is flush with talent, the group has a tendency to chase pitches out of the zone, and they don’t draw walks at a high rate. The Braves ranked 28th in MLB in on-base percentage (.309) during the regular season, often opting for an aggressive approach at the plate rather than a patient one. That could prove costly in October against some of the best pitchers in the sport, where slowing the game down and getting runners on base by any means necessary will be crucial.
5. New York Yankees
Biggest strength: Elite pitching rotation
Biggest weakness: Offense (without Aaron Judge), high strikeout rates
Yankees starting pitchers led MLB with a 3.30 ERA this season, and they’ll have one of the best rotations in the postseason with Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon set to take the mound in October. The bullpen has been a bit inconsistent, but they should be able to ride their starting rotation deep into games. The biggest weakness for the Yankees is their lineup, particularly without Aaron Judge in the mix. New York had the sixth-most strikeouts this season and were tied for 11th in MLB with a .720 OPS. With Judge out of the lineup, however, their OPS falls to a .690 mark, which would be 29th in MLB.
6. San Diego Padres
Biggest strength: Elite bullpen
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Padres’ bullpen has been as reliable as they come this season, and the team flexes multiple elite relievers who they can reliably turn the ball over to in the later innings in Mason Miller, Yuki Matsui and Adrian Morejon, among others. San Diego has shaken off a slow start to the year and are playing at an extremely high level heading into the postseason. The offense is alive again after a dreadful first couple of months of the season, with players like Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill having been among MLB’s best second-half performers at the plate. The starting pitching will be the x-factor in October, however. With Casey Mize landing on the IL, their options in the rotation are even thinner. Remaining competitive within the first six innings will be crucial for the Padres, whose starting pitchers rank 21st in MLB with a 4.42 ERA this year.
7. Chicago Cubs
Biggest strength: Dominant lineup
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The Cubs have had MLB’s best offense this season, leading the league in OPS (.767), walks (674), runs scored (850) and slugging percentage (.428). They’ve been particularly elite since the All-Star break, logging a .797 OPS in their last 66 games. With Pete Crow-Armstrong playing at an MVP level and Alex Bregman having enjoyed a monster second half, the Cubs’ offense will be tough to shut down in October. Of course, they’ll need their pitching to live up to their end of the bargain, which it’s struggled to do this season. Chicago’s starting pitching has been disappointing and plagued by injuries. The starting rotation ranks 18th in MLB with a 4.27 ERA this year and have surrendered the third-most home runs (142).
8. Boston Red Sox
Biggest strength: Elite pitching
Biggest weakness: Inconsistent offense
The Red Sox’s pitching as a whole has been excellent. Boston’s bullpen owns a league-best 3.00 ERA this season, and no group of relievers in MLB has surrendered fewer home runs (55). Their starters have been great, too, ranking eighth in the league with a 3.92 ERA, and they boast a solid mix of veterans (Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez) and young, emerging starters (Payton Tolle and Jake Bennett). Offensively, however, the Red Sox have been prone to spells of inconsistency. They started the season ice cold before enjoying a scalding hot summer streak, but they’ve come crashing back down to earth in the final month of the season. The Red Sox rank dead last in MLB in OPS (.651) throughout the month of September, and they’re batting a league-worst .219 in that span.
9. Cleveland Guardians
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Lack of power
The Guardians starting pitching has been a top-10 unit this season, ranking ninth in ERA (3.93) and fifth in strikeouts (878). Parker Messick has been superb in his first full season in MLB, and Gavin Williams has emerged as one of the league’s best strikeout pitchers. Cleveland will feel confident with those two spearheading the rotation, but they may struggle to get the run support required to take advantage of their quality starters. The Guardians rank 24th in MLB with 678 runs scored, 26th in OPS (.696) and 27th in home runs (162) this season. If they can’t come up with some big at-bats, it won’t matter how effective their pitching is in October.
10. Philadelphia Phillies
Biggest strength: Starting pitching
Biggest weakness: Defense, bullpen
The Phillies have one of the best starting rotations in MLB, but they’ve been plagued by some underperforming position players and a lackluster bullpen. There’s arguably no better trio of starters in MLB than Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and Jesús Luzardo. The team’s starting rotation ranks seventh in the league with a 3.80 ERA, but their bullpen ranks 21st in ERA (4.43). Defensively, the Phillies have been atrocious, too. Only the Athletics have fewer defensive runs saved than the Phillies’ -43, according to the Fielding Bible, and the infield has been a serious concern, with Trea Turner, Bryce Harper and Alec Bohm all ranking among the bottom 26 defensive players (of 270 qualified players) in MLB in terms of outs above average, per Statcast. Defensive shortcomings and mishaps could prove highly costly in October, and that’s an area that’s plagued Philadelphia all season.
11. Chicago White Sox
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
The White Sox have a potent lineup and are the only team in MLB that have three players who hit 30 or more home runs in Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery. Chicago hit the fifth-most home runs this season (211) and scored the fifth-most runs (776). While the offense is among the league’s best in terms of power, the White Sox starting pitching is a serious concern. The starting rotation posted a season ERA of 4.60 (fourth-worst in MLB), a 1.34 WHIP (sixth-worst in MLB) and recorded the third-fewest strikeouts of any starting rotation in the league. Chicago’s starters also threw the fewest innings in MLB this season, often struggling to get deep into games before the baton was passed to the bullpen. If the starting rotation can’t keep runs off the board, it might not matter how explosive their lineup can be.
12. Houston Astros
Biggest strength: Power hitting
Biggest weakness: Starting pitching
Yordan Alvarez is likely to win the AL MVP, and he’s the type of hitter teams will not be eager to pitch to in October. No team in MLB hit more home runs than the Astros, who hit 226. In addition to Alvarez’s 42, Houston had four other players with 20-plus homers, including Christian Walker (29), Isaac Paredes (25), Jeremy Peña (22) and Cam Smith (21). They don’t have much to worry about offensively, but their lineup will need to produce in order to ease the burden on their starting rotation, which has largely struggled this year. Hunter Brown remains a reliable ace, but beyond him there’s a lack of experience and talent within the rotation. Astros starters ranked 27th in MLB with a 4.81 ERA and 1.40 WHIP, both of which were the worst among all teams that qualified for the postseason, and they walked the most batters in MLB this season. If the lineup can’t make up for the rotation’s shortcomings, it could be a short postseason stint for Houston this year.
Karl Rasmussen is a staff writer for Sports Illustrated. A University of Oregon alum who joined SI in February 2023, his work has appeared on 12up and ClutchPoints. Rasmussen is a loyal Tottenham, Jets, Yankees and Ducks fan.
Follow Karlras920

Riley was picked in the 1st round of the 2015 MLB Draft.

On Monday, the Philadelphia Phillies are off following Sunday’s 7-3 win over the Tampa Bay Rays.
With the victory, they clinched a spot in the 2026 MLB playoffs.
The Phillies will now go to Atlanta for a three-game series with the Braves at Truist Park (starting on Tuesday).
Bryce Harper Makes Honest Statement
Bryce Harper has had many battles with the Braves over his career.
Ahead of the series, he met with the media.
Harper (via Chad Bishop of AJC): “I love playing here. This is one of my favorite parks to play in. I love the field. I love the setup of it. I enjoy coming into Atlanta and playing. Obviously, the crowd’s in it. They love their team. And it’s just a lot of fun coming in here and playing.”

Harper is in the middle of his 8th season with the Phillies.
He led the franchise to the 2022 World Series.

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA — Yes, these Phillies.
The same core that has reached the postseason five consecutive years, yet hasn't won a playoff series since 2023, has another opportunity to finish what it started.
But Bryce Harper sees some differences in this version of the Phillies, even if many of the names are familiar.
"I think they're different, but they have a little bit of the same DNA," Harper said Monday at Truist Park. "We have a lot of the same and similar DNA that we've had the last couple years, with a sprinkle of a couple other guys."
Those additions, along with the growth of several returning players, could help determine whether Philadelphia's latest postseason appearance ends differently from its previous two.
The most obvious change is in the bullpen.
Over the last two postseasons, Phillies relievers have combined for a 6.82 ERA, a 1.65 WHIP and six home runs allowed in 30 1/3 innings. Their ERA jumps to 11.42 when pitching with a lead.
News
Those numbers help explain why Philadelphia hasn't advanced beyond the NLDS in either of its last two appearances.
This year's relief group looks considerably different. José Alvarado is the only remaining member of the Phillies' 2023 bullpen, and after posting a 5.86 ERA this season, he isn't expected to handle the most important late-inning assignments.
Instead, Philadelphia has Jhoan Duran at the back end, with Jonathan Bowlan, Alex McFarlane and Chase Shugart among the newer faces who could be asked to get the ball to their closer.
The Phillies haven't seen how this group will respond together in October. That uncertainty leaves them with questions, but at least they'll be trying to solve a familiar problem with a different group of pitchers.
The offense, meanwhile, has undergone fewer changes. Philadelphia still relies heavily on Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Trea Turner, with Alec Bohm and Bryson Stott providing much of the production behind them.
And that group has something to prove.
Of the 12 teams that played multiple postseason series across 2024 and 2025, the Phillies had the lowest batting average, the lowest average with runners in scoring position and the highest chase rate.
Too often, Philadelphia has struggled to put the ball in play when it has an opportunity to score. It was one of the reasons the club acquired Luis Arraez in August, but a left ankle sprain suffered during the final week of the regular season will keep him off the Wild Card roster.
That puts more responsibility on the returning hitters to sustain rallies against an Atlanta pitching staff that begins the series with Chris Sale and Tyler Mahle.
Bohm and Stott enter the postseason swinging the bat well, something Turner believes reflects the growth he's witnessed within the clubhouse this year.
"I think it was just kind of cool to see guys struggle at times and then pull themselves out of it at times," Turner said. "It didn't go as well as it could have gone for a lot of us."
He pointed specifically to Bohm, whose difficult start gave way to a productive final several months.
"He's been such a good player for a long time, and then this second half or the last two-thirds of the season, he's been really, really good for us," Turner said.
But the Phillies have also introduced a different kind of hitter into the lower part of their lineup.
Justin Crawford, who made his major league debut earlier this season, has given Philadelphia another player capable of reaching base, putting pressure on the defense and delivering in important situations.
From June 14 through the end of the regular season, Crawford hit .294, the 15th-highest average in baseball among players who appeared in at least 80 games during that span. He ranked third among rookies who met that qualification.
His production with runners in scoring position was even more striking.
Crawford hit .491 in those situations over that stretch, the highest average among 109 players who met the same games-played requirement. His 1.131 OPS with runners in scoring position ranked fifth.
He won't necessarily start every postseason game. Crawford shares center-field duties with Derek Hill, whose speed, defense and production against left-handed pitching give interim manager Don Mattingly another way to construct his lineup.
Hill has made quite an impression on Harper.
"He's just a professional, I would say. He's got a professional mindset," Harper said. "Obviously having his pops, coming from a big-league family, I think that helps a lot."
Harper went a step further when discussing Hill's arrival, which came in a June trade with the Chicago White Sox.
"I think it's one of the better moves Dave has made for our organization bringing him in," Harper said, referring to president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski.
His praise extended well beyond Hill's production. Harper singled out the way the outfielder prepares, backs up bases, looks for opportunities to advance and helps Philadelphia's younger players.
"He's a gamer. He plays the game the right way, and you need guys like that on your team," Harper said.
Hill is also part of a trio that has developed a close bond away from the field.
Along with Bryan De La Cruz and Edmundo Sosa, he belongs to "Team Blessed," a group built around their shared faith and a competitive batting-cage routine during games. All three have contributed in important moments throughout the season, frequently coming off the bench without the benefit of regular at-bats.
Harper mentioned Hill and De La Cruz specifically when asked what makes this club different from previous Phillies postseason teams. Both have given Philadelphia additional options against left-handed pitching, something it lacked earlier in the year.
And Harper believes players in those supporting roles can end up being the ones everyone remembers.
"It's funny to look back on a lot of postseasons in baseball history," Harper said. "Not many of the superstar players play to their ability."
Harper himself is a notable exception.
Among the 109 hitters in postseason history with at least 200 plate appearances, his .986 OPS ranks third, trailing only Carlos Beltrán and Albert Pujols. His .596 slugging percentage is fourth.
But his point wasn't about the stars who have delivered in October. It was about the players whose contributions nobody saw coming.
Consider Travis Ishikawa, a part-time first baseman who found himself playing left field for the 2014 San Francisco Giants. In Game 5 of the NLCS, Ishikawa hit a three-run, walk-off homer against the Cardinals to send San Francisco to the World Series.
That's the type of player Harper had in mind when discussing Philadelphia's reserves.
"You never know who the October hero is going to be," Harper said. "Then you get to the end and you're like, man, that guy had a great postseason and you might never hear from him again."
Hill, De La Cruz, Sosa and Crawford will have opportunities to write their own postseason stories. For some, it will be their first chance to experience an October environment that Harper knows well.
His advice is to avoid treating it as a different game.
"All the work that you put in during the season and all the work that you put in to get you to this point, all that doesn't matter," Harper said. "It's the same game that we've been playing. It just might get a little bit quicker or might speed up on you a little bit if you let it."
That doesn't mean the veteran slugger wants his younger teammates to ignore the occasion.
"If you can really try to just enjoy the moment, I don't know, you could go 0-for-4 tomorrow or you could go 0-for-5 tomorrow or you can go 3-for-4 with two homers and win a game," Harper said. "If you just really take in the moment, take in the opportunity, there's no greater feeling."
The Phillies have considerable postseason experience, but this season has tested them in ways their more recent teams haven't necessarily encountered.
They began 9-19, underwent a managerial change and spent much of the year rearranging their pitching staff because of injuries and inconsistent performances.
There are similarities to 2022, when Philadelphia also changed managers after a difficult start before making an improbable run to the World Series. That team didn't secure its postseason berth until Oct. 3 and entered the playoffs having gone 11-14 in September.
Turner wasn't part of that club. He joined the Phillies the following offseason, and much of what stood out to him about this year's team had less to do with the final results than the way his teammates responded to their own struggles.
He recalled a recent conversation about Schwarber, who was still working through issues with his swing during the final days of the regular season.
"He's hit 380 homers in his career, and one of the best hitters in the game, and he's just not satisfied," Turner said.
For Turner, that restlessness says something about the veteran players who have been together through several disappointing postseason exits.
"Just seeing guys kind of manage their situations and want to compete and want to get back out there and just loving the game, I think that was pretty cool from a team standpoint," he said.
It's a perspective that comes from watching the same players through different stages of their careers. As Harper acknowledged, they're getting older. Stott has grown into a more established hitter, Bohm's future in Philadelphia is uncertain, and the club has brought in new players to complement a core that has been trying to win a championship for years.
The Phillies have invested heavily in their starting rotation, traded for a closer last year they believe can handle the biggest innings and introduced players who could give their offense a different look. But much of their postseason success will still depend on familiar names producing in situations where they've struggled before.
Harper, now preparing for his ninth postseason in 15 major league seasons, understands how rare those opportunities can become.
He brought up Hall-of-Fame quarterback Dan Marino, who reached the Super Bowl early in his career but never returned, as an example of how little a player's previous success guarantees about what comes next.
The Phillies have reached October five straight years. That doesn't mean they'll keep getting chances.
"I'm very lucky," Harper said. "Obviously I haven't got to the point where I want to be or our team hasn't either, but just to be in these moments, just to be given the opportunity to be here, I'm so grateful for that. It motivates me to get to these points."
Philadelphia arrives in Atlanta with many of the same stars, some new faces and the experience of a regular season that nearly slipped away from it.
Harper knows what he wants this group to accomplish. But after all the postseason games he's played, he's learned there's no telling which teammate might deliver the moment that gets them there.
"It's a cool opportunity for a lot of guys that have never played here," he said. "You could end up being a hero after having just an absolute terrible year."
Push for the playoffs coverage on NBC Sports Philadelphia is presented by Toyota, proud partner of the Philadelphia Phillies.

item.title: [fansided.com] Evaluating the Hall of Fame trajectories of Shohei Ohtani and MLB’s postseason stars
item.dc:creator: Jake Elman

item.content:encoded:
Back in July, we celebrated the All-Star Game by looking at which participants had the best chance of eventually earning induction into the Hall of Fame. The likes of Bryce Harper, Justin Verlander, and Mike Trout all were locks, and rightfully so.
But as the MLB playoffs prepare to kick off, Verlander and Trout are once again sitting at home. Harper and the Phillies survived a near-collapse to secure a Wild Card seed, and he’s one of many postseason participants who could — and in his case, should — find themselves in the Hall of Fame one day.
Besides the obvious counting stats, what makes a Hall of Famer? As we’ve previously noted, baseball fans have recently accepted 40 bWAR as the standard for a remarkable career. Immaculate Grid is to thank on that front, even if there are players who have cleared that mark but don’t feel like Hall of Famers. Astros shortstop Carlos Correa, who is injured but has a 47.1 bWAR, is a perfect example, and he didn’t crack our list.
Instead, let’s turn our attention to someone who may very well become the second unanimous electee when his time comes.
Honorable mention: The Shohei Ohtani tier
Barring any unprecedented rule changes, Hall of Fame candidates must have 10 full seasons worth of experience for eligibility. That means Shohei Ohtani would technically be ineligible if he retired tomorrow, so he won’t land in the “lock” tier.
But Ohtani has always been a unicorn, so him having his own category makes all too much sense. We can all agree that, at this time next year, Ohtani should be a lock on that list.
Not yet eligible, but…
These guys don’t get their own table, but we wanted to address their situations ahead of the playoffs.
- Aroldis Chapman, P, Boston Red Sox: Off the numbers alone, Chapman and his 402 saves (ninth all-time) likely warrant induction. However, he also served a 30-game suspension in 2016 for violating the league’s domestic violence policy. It’s difficult to envision him earning the 75 percent required for election. Recent voting trends don’t work in favor of those who have been suspended for performance-enhancing drugs (more on that soon) or off-field incidents.
- Cam Schlittler, SP, New York Yankees and Jacob Misirowski, SP, Milwaukee Brewers: We’re lumping these two together because both will be trending during the playoffs. Just because these two are likely to win their league’s respective Cy Young Awards doesn’t mean they’re guaranteed a spot in Cooperstown. Heck, we don’t even know if they’ll pitch long enough to appear on a ballot! But, you know how baseball fans are.
- Fernando Tatis Jr., 2B/RF, San Diego Padres: As things currently stand, Tatis has no chance of getting into the Hall of Fame. Voters have made it clear that those who serve PED-related suspensions, as Tatis did in 2022, aren’t welcome in Cooperstown unless they buy a ticket. That said, we’re including him here
- Tarik Skubal, SP, Los Angeles Dodgers: Skubal became the 23rd pitcher in MLB history to win multiple Cy Young Awards, which will appeal to voters who prefer the "dominant" peak. But we’d like to see at least two or three more years of him being at least above-average. He’s also only seven seasons in, so he has a lot of work left.
On pace to make it into Cooperstown
- Alex Bregman, Chicago Cubs - 48.9 bWAR
- Matt Olson, Atlanta Braves - 44.2 bWAR
- Yordan Alvarez, DH, Houston Astros - 30.5 bWAR
These three have team success, specifically at least one World Series ring, working in their favor. Alvarez is likely to win AL MVP, and the 29-year-old is young enough that clearing 40 bWAR shouldn’t be an issue so long as healthy.
Bregman turns 33 next March, and his bWAR is likely far greater than you’d have guessed. But is he truly on a Hall of Fame trajectory? He's nowhere close to 2,000 hits (1,411) or 300 home runs (237), both of which are vital numbers when playing the hot corner.
Consider, though, that Bregman has averaged 24 home runs, 84 RBIs, 32 doubles, and 4.6 bWAR over the last five years. He’s under contract through 2030, and exceeded all of those numbers (28 home runs, 93 RBIs, 33 doubles, and 5.8 bWAR) this season.
If Bregman were to continue averaging those numbers, he’d end the 2031 season with 333 home runs, roughly 2,200 hits, and 481 doubles. Oh, and his bWAR would be right around 72.0, so we imagine he’d be a first-ballot inductee.
Unfortunately for him and Olson, the possibility of a work stoppage could have a monumental impact on their final counting stats. Which leads us into…
Borderline veterans
- Giancarlo Stanton, New York Yankees - 47.0 bWAR
- Zack Wheeler, Philadelphia Phillies - 46.6 bWAR
- Gerrit Cole, SP, New York Yankees - 45.8 bWAR
- Christian Yelich, Milwaukee Brewers - 45.1 bWAR
- Xander Bogaerts, SS, San Diego Padres - 44.3 bWAR
- Max Fried, P, New York Yankees - 32.3 bWAR
- Kyle Schwarber, OF/DH, Philadelphia Phillies - 22.3 bWAR
Stanton and Schwarber’s cases are likely dependent on whether they surpass 500 home runs. The latter will enter next season at 385 homers, and he turns 34 in March. But the looming work stoppage could significantly affect his chances of reaching 400 anytime soon.
As for Stanton, multiple lower-body injuries limited him to three homers in 24 games. Although he has 466 career home runs, the 2017 NL MVP turns 37 in November and is a free agent after next year.
The only members of the 500-home run club who aren’t in the Hall of Fame are either ineligible or have ties to performance-enhancing drugs. It’d be pretty remarkable if Schwarber and Stanton both cleared the historic total yet fell short of Cooperstown.
Personally, Wheeler and Cole are probably the only ones who will have a legitimate Hall of Fame résumé when they become eligible. The rest of those guys are Hall of Very Good at best. Much like Skubal, we need two or three more elite seasons from Fried before we’d even consider voting for him.
Go ahead and make the Hall of Fame plaque
- Mookie Betts, Los Angeles Dodgers - 79.0 bWAR
- Freddie Freeman, Los Angeles Dodgers - 66.8 bWAR
- Paul Goldschmidt, New York Yankees - 65.1 bWAR
- Aaron Judge, New York Yankees - 64.2 bWAR
- Manny Machado, San Diego Padres - 63.3 bWAR
- Chris Sale, Atlanta Braves - 62.7 bWAR
- José Ramírez, Cleveland Guardians - 60.3 bWAR
- Bryce Harper, Philadelphia Phillies - 56.9 bWAR
- Jose Altuve, Houston Astros - 53.4 bWAR
Outside of Goldschmidt and Sale, none of these names are overly surprising. And no, the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal shouldn’t impact Altuve, especially not after Carlos Beltrán just entered the Hall of Fame.
Goldschmidt currently ranks 143rd on the all-time bWAR list, and only 31 men above him aren’t already enshrined. But of the 20 who are or were eligible, most came up short for PED or off-field reasons. The question then becomes whether he’s wearing a Diamondbacks or Cardinals cap, or if he opts for the blank hat.
Although Sale turns 38 next March, he has a lifetime 2.95 ERA and 2,779 strikeouts, putting him within range of reaching 3,000. There’s absolutely no reason why he shouldn’t be a first-ballot selection.
As for the rest? You know a Hall of Famer when you see one, and they more than meet the expectations.
